/data/data/<app>/files/<subPath> - /storage/emulated/0/Android/data/<app>/files/.config/<subPath> (if EXTERNAL_STORAGE set) - /storage/emulated/0/Android/data/<app>/files/<subPath> SESSION scope: - /data/data/<app>/cache/.config/<subPath> - Plus Linux-style fallbacks. Fallback (unknown OS) USER scope: - ~/.<app>/<subPath> HOST scope: - $PWD/.config/<app>/<subPath>
docs.title: Filesystem search paths (FileConfigStorage)

docs.text: When you ask for a ConfigEntry (or just its value) by providing a key, the library starts searching. The normal method is using a layered stack, sorted by the aforementioned scopes. At top, if enabled, is the cache layer, at RUNTIME scope. Below it follow the other scopes, down to the PRODUCT scope, where you can find the defaults layer. For each layer, the respective configuration source is asked whether it has an entry matching the key. The topmost layer which has a valid entry wins, and you get the ConfigEntry it has found. If you asked for just the value, not the full ConfigEntry, then the library tries to return the data found in the Java class matching the type of value you asked for (e.g. Boolean, Integer, byte array).
docs.title: Layered Stack

docs.text: Note the mention of valid data. You can, and should, provide a ConfigSchema which declares the expected entries, and some information about them.
docs.title: validation

docs.text: A schema entry typically includes: - Key : The hierarchical name of the configuration entry. - Type : The expected data type (e.g., STRING , NUMBER , BOOLEAN , BYTES , DATE , DURATION ). - Default Value : A fallback value used if the entry is missing from all other layers. - Description : Documentation for the entry, used in reports and UI. - Flags : Metadata like MANDATORY , SECRET , or HIDDEN . - Validation Rules : Patterns or ranges (e.g., regex for strings, min/max for numbers) to ensure data integrity.
docs.title: Schema Components

docs.text: When a configuration is accessed: 1. Discovery : The library searches for the key through the layered stack. 2. Type Enforcement : If a schema is active, the raw data from a ConfigSource is converted to the type specified in the schema. If conversion fails (e.g., "abc" for a NUMBER ), the entry is considered invalid, and the search continues in lower priority layers. 3. Constraint Checking : The converted value is checked against validation rules (regex, ranges, enums). 4. Outcome : - Valid : The entry is returned and potentially cached. - Invalid : By default, the library logs a warning and skips the invalid entry, continuing the search in lower priority layers. - Missing Mandatory : If a MANDATORY entry is not found in any layer (including the default layer), a ConfigException is thrown upon access.
docs.title: The Validation Process

docs.text: When a ConfigSchema is activated for a Configuration : - It populates the Default Layer (PRODUCT scope) with any default values defined in the schema. - It provides the metadata required for automated documentation and schema export. - It acts as a gatekeeper for all data entering the Configuration facade, ensuring type safety.
docs.title: Schema Activation

docs.text: There's two different aspects to changes. First, getting notifications when the value of a config entry changes. This is actively checking, even polling, for changes, to notify your code about such events. It checks across different ConfigSources, formats, and the like. mConfig provides a subscription mechanism via subscribeToUpdates(Consumer<ConfigLocation>) . This allows applications (and tools like the mconfig monitor command) to react to configuration changes in real-time. Second, the automated cache flush for some config sources. For most, reading is not much effort; but certain ones - especially files and parsing their formats - are not that cheap. So these are read, parsed, and then cached for some time. But the cache should not stay indefinitely, it needs to detect changes and/or refresh automatically. → ConfigFeature.UPDATE_CHECK_FREQUENCY_MS
docs.title: Changes & Monitoring

docs.text: mConfig uses these concepts for separation of concerns: ConfigStorage ( ConfigStorageInterface ) is an access medium: filesystem, classpath/JAR resources, Windows registry, environment variables, network services such as ZooKeeper or Vault. It provides the technical access. Examples: FileConfigStorage , JARConfigSource , EnvVarConfigStorage , WindowsRegistryConfigSource , VaultConfigStorage , SchemaDefaultConfigStorage . ConfigFormat ( ConfigFormatInterface ) is how a configuration is encoded inside a blob-like storage: Java properties, JSON, YAML, TOML, INI, and so on. Files, specifically, come in a number of different formats; the format handles the actual parsing and writing. The Windows registry is a storage, not a format; like environment variables and Vault, it converts its own value types and needs no format. ConfigLocation : a place where a configuration may be found: storage, storage-specific handle (e.g. a directory), and scope. The ConfigSearchList of a factory is a list of these. ConfigSource : a ConfigLocation that has been instantiated, so there is a layer to it. ConfigLayer : the concrete data read from one location, mapped to hierarchical keys. For blob-like storages (files, ZooKeeper BLOBs, JAR resources) a format produces the layer; storages with structured data of their own (Windows registry, environment variables, Vault) produce it themselves. Module naming : a module named mConfigSource<Name> (e.g. mConfigSourceFilesystem , mConfigSourceVault ) provides a storage, despite "Source" in its name. erDiagram Configuration }|--|| ConfigFactory : "comes from" ConfigFactory ||--|| ConfigSearchList : has ConfigSearchList ||--|{ ConfigLocation : contains ConfigLocation }|--|| ConfigStorage : "accessed through" Configuration ||--|{ ConfigLayer : "stacks" ConfigLayer ||--|| ConfigSource : "read from" ConfigSource ||--|| ConfigLocation : "is an instantiated" ConfigStorage ||--o{ ConfigFormat : "may use" Configuration ||--o| ConfigSchema : "may use" ConfigSchema ||--o{ ConfigSchemaEntry : contains Configuration : the API interface to access configurations; produces/keeps ConfigEntry instances, and provides simple access to the values. A Configuration is built by going through the search list of its ConfigFactory; for each location, the storage adds the layers it finds, sorted by scope. A Configuration object is a way to access configurations in a uniform way.
docs.title: Behind the Scenes

docs.text: The ConfigFactoryBuilder gathers and combines all the settings. It creates a ConfigFactoryInstanceContext and a ConfigFactory to use it. The ConfigFactoryInstanceContext is passed to several objects the ConfigFactory uses, so they can get their respective features, settings, access to a logger, and so on - it is an internally shared resource.
docs.title: Anchor

docs.text: mConfig has built-in support for sensitive data such as passwords, API keys, and private certificates.
docs.title: Security and Secrets

docs.text: Config entries marked as secrets in the ConfigSchema are automatically handled with care: - Their toString() representation is redacted ( [REDACTED] ). (using stars could be ambiguous) - They are stored in specialized SecretConfigEntryLeaf objects. - In-memory storage uses byte[] or char[] to allow for clearing the data after use.
docs.title: Secret Redaction

docs.text: For programmatically accessing secrets, mConfig provides the SecretValue interface. This allows retrieving the sensitive data without it being accidentally converted to a standard String that might linger in the Java String Pool. SecretValue password = config.getSecret("database/password"); byte[] rawBytes = password.getValue(); // ... use and then potentially clear the bytes
docs.title: The SecretValue API

docs.text: Not all configuration is text-based. mConfig supports Binary Large Objects (BLOBs) for things like license files, binary keys, or certificates.
docs.title: Binary Data (BLOBs)

docs.text: In modern formats like JSON and YAML, binary data can be embedded directly. - YAML uses the standard !!binary tag. - JSON uses Base64 encoded strings. If a ConfigSchema is provided that marks a key as BYTES type, mConfig will automatically decode the Base64 string into a byte array.
docs.title: Hierarchical BLOBs

docs.text: For legacy support or specific use cases, an entire file can be treated as a single binary blob. This uses the binary_file format and is accessed via the empty string key ( "" ). // Retrieving an entire .bin file as a single blob Configuration licenseCfg = factory.getConfig("license"); byte[] licenseData = licenseCfg.getBytes("");
docs.title: Flat Binary Files

docs.text: If there is no ConfigEntry found at any layer, and no specific default is found, the reaction is determined by the ConfigFeature flags set. (a) return a generic default value depending on the type (b) throw ConfigException (runtime exception type) (c) return "null" as ConfigEntry handle, your own code wants to handle the details. — this will still cause an exception if you are asking for the value only. It is recommended, though, that you provide for each config entry you are reading a default value which is sensible and useful in the context of your use case.
docs.title: Failure Handling

docs.text: 2.2 Priorities and Hierarchies ¶ 2.2.1 Search List and Priority ¶ The ConfigFactory maintains an ordered Search List of locations. This order is crucial for two reasons: Finding and Creating Configurations: When looking for a configuration or creating a new one (e.g., via ConfigUtil.whereToPutMyFiles ), mConfig searches through the list and picks the first matching writeable location. Thus, entries earlier in the search list have higher priority for discovery and creation. Layered Overrides (Reading): Configurations are composed of multiple layers. Layers from more specific Scopes (e.g., RUNTIME ) always override more generic scopes (e.g., SYSTEM ). Within the same scope , however, the search list determines priority: layers from locations appearing later in the search list are added later to the configuration stack and thus override layers from locations appearing earlier in the same scope. 2.2.2 Potential (Candidate) Locations vs. Instantiated Layers ¶ An important architectural aspect of mConfig is the separation between candidate search locations and active configuration layers: Candidate Locations ( ConfigLocation via ConfigFactory.getSearchList() ): The factory's search list contains all potential ConfigLocation s evaluated by active storage providers (e.g., standard filesystem paths across scopes). Candidate directories are retained in the search list even if they do not exist on disk at initialization time. When a missing directory or file is created at runtime, storages that watch their locations (such as the filesystem storage) detect it and bind the new source. Active Locations ( ConfigLocation via Configuration.getSourceLocations() ): Represents only the locations that currently exist and contributed active data layers to a specific Configuration handle. Active Layers ( ConfigLayerInterface ): The concrete in-memory representations of parsed configuration entries contributing to the configuration stack. These are internal; library code reaches them via LayeredConfiguration.getLayers() , which is not part of the public Configuration API. Discovered Configurations ( ConfigDiscoveryInfo via ConfigFactory.listAvailableConfigurations() ): Scans all candidate locations in getSearchList() and returns metadata for configuration files that currently exist.
docs.title: 2.2 Priorities and Hierarchies

docs.text: 2.3 Configuration Schemas ¶ Configuration schemas define the contract for a set of configuration entries. They specify what keys are expected, their data types, default values, validation rules, and other metadata. 2.3.1 Overview ¶ A schema ensures that the configuration data used by the application is valid and consistent. When a configuration is loaded (e.g., via getConfig(name) ), mConfig attempts to bind it to a matching schema. 2.3.1.1 Benefits of using Schemas ¶ Validation : Automatically check if values match expected types and patterns. Defaults : Provide fallback values if none are found in any configuration layer. Documentation : Automatically generate documentation for configuration entries. Type Safety : Preserve data types (e.g., Integer, Boolean) throughout the configuration stack. Security : Identify which entries contain sensitive data (secrets). 2.3.2 Example ¶ Minimal example (single schema entry with a default): [ { "KEY": "server/port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080, "DESCRIPTION": "Listening port" } ] Named schema example (multiple entries): { "my-app-config": { "NAME": "my-app-config", "ENTRIES": [ { "KEY": "server/host", "TYPE": "STRING", "DEFAULT": "127.0.0.1" }, { "KEY": "server/port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080 } ] } } 2.3.3 Schema Structure ¶ Schemas are typically defined in JSON format. A schema file can contain a single schema or multiple named schemas. 2.3.3.1 Schema Entry Properties ¶ Each entry in a schema (within the ENTRIES list) can have the following properties: Property Type Description KEY String The hierarchical path of the entry (e.g., database/host ). TYPE String The data type: STRING , NUMBER , BOOLEAN , BYTES , MULTIPLE_STRINGS , ENUM , ENUM_SET , URI , FILEPATH , DATE , TIME , DATETIME . DESCRIPTION String Human-readable description or Resource Bundle key for localized description. (Optional) DEFAULT (any) The default value used if no other value is provided. (Optional) PATTERN String A validation pattern (Regex, range specification, or enum list). (Optional) SECRET Boolean If true , the entry holds a cryptographic secret or credential: it is redacted in logs, kept out of the JVM String pool, and retrieved via getSecret() . (Optional, defaults to false ) SENSITIVE Boolean If true , the entry holds information that must not be disclosed, typically personal data under GDPR. Defined but not yet enforced — see below. (Optional, defaults to false ) HIDDEN Boolean If true , the entry is hidden from automatic documentation. (Optional, defaults to false ) FLAGS Array Declarative markers for the entry: MANDATORY , READ_ONLY , WRITE_ONLY , SECRET , SENSITIVE . Not all are enforced yet — see below. ARITY String The number of allowed occurrences (e.g., 1 , 0..1 , 1..* ). (Optional; see defaults below) MANDATORY Object (Optional) Block for future-proofing and strict requirements. Note this is the block , distinct from the MANDATORY entry in FLAGS . See below. AFTER String (Optional) For temporal types, value must be after this (ISO format or now ). BEFORE String (Optional) For temporal types, value must be before this (ISO format or now ). REQUIRE_OFFSET Boolean (Optional) For DATETIME , requires an offset (e.g., +02:00 or Z ). Property names are matched case-insensitively, so "KEY" and "key" are equivalent. Boolean values ¶ An entry of TYPE BOOLEAN accepts true/false , yes/no , on/off and 1/0 , in any case and with surrounding blanks; a DEFAULT of "on" is valid. Any other value, an empty one included, does not match the schema. Such a value is skipped when read: the next layer, or finally the DEFAULT , applies, so a typing error in one file does not switch a feature off. Writing such a value through put() is rejected. (Up to 0.8.16 the check accepted true and false only.) Without a schema, getBoolean() uses the first value found and throws ConfigException ( CONVERSION_FAILURE ) if it is not one of these literals. See LENIENT_BOOLEAN_CONVERSION for the plain Java behaviour. Confidentiality markers: SECRET and SENSITIVE ¶ These mark two different kinds of confidentiality, and most entries that are SECRET are also SENSITIVE — though rarely the reverse. In short: SECRET is for cryptographic secrets and passwords, SENSITIVE for information that must not leak into view, such as personal data. See Secret and Sensitive for the full model, including which storage places will accept which kind of data. Both markers suppress disclosure of the value only. The storage location of a marked entry stays traceable through getScope() , getLocation() and getURI() , so protected data remains findable, correctable and erasable. Which markers are enforced today ¶ The FLAGS array is accepted and parsed, but the library does not yet act on every marker in it: Marker Enforced? Notes MANDATORY yes via FLAGS ; drives default arity and presence validation SECRET yes only via the SECRET property , not via FLAGS (see the warning below) SENSITIVE no recognised and stored; no redaction or export suppression yet READ_ONLY no recognised and stored; writes are not blocked yet WRITE_ONLY no recognised and stored; reads are not blocked yet Warning: "FLAGS": ["SECRET"] does not currently mark an entry as secret. The flag is stored but is not consulted by the secrets handling, which reads only the separate SECRET property. Always write "SECRET": true . Using the flag alone means the value is not protected — no redaction, no SecretValue , no wiping. Since 0.8.15, loading a schema logs a WARNING for each entry that uses a marker without effect: SECRET in FLAGS without "SECRET": true (the value is not protected), and SENSITIVE , READ_ONLY or WRITE_ONLY (not enforced yet). SECRET in FLAGS next to "SECRET": true is redundant and not reported. 0.9.0 will be stricter. 2.3.3.2 Arity ( ARITY ) ¶ The ARITY property defines the constraints on the number of elements for an entry. This is especially useful for MULTIPLE_STRINGS and ENUM_SET types. Exact number : "ARITY": "3" (exactly 3 items required). Range : "ARITY": "1..5" (minimum 1, maximum 5 items). Open-ended : "ARITY": "1..*" or "ARITY": "1..n" (at least 1 item, no upper limit). Defaults : Mandatory entries: 1 Optional entries: 0..1 List types ( MULTIPLE_STRINGS , ENUM_SET ): 0..* (optional) or 1..* (mandatory). 2.3.3.3 Validation Patterns ( PATTERN ) ¶ Validation patterns depend on the TYPE of the entry: STRING : A Java Regular Expression. Compiled with Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS by default, supporting Unicode property escapes like \p{L} . NUMBER : Mathematical Interval Notation : Supports [min, max] , (min, max) , [min, max) , and (min, max] . Example: [1024, 65535] . Predefined Aliases : Unsigned: uint8 (0-255), uint16 , uint32 , uint64 . Signed: int8 (-128 to 127), int16 , int32 , int64 , and custom bit-widths like int7 , int15 , int31 , int63 . ENUM / ENUM_SET : A pipe-separated list of valid options. Example: DEBUG|INFO|WARN|ERROR . URI : A valid URI string (RFC 3986). FILEPATH : A valid path on the filesystem. Path Validation Flags : Can be placed inside the MANDATORY block for semantic checks: EXISTS : true (path must exist) IS_DIRECTORY : true (path must be a directory) IS_FILE : true (path must be a regular file) CAN_WRITE : true (path must be writable) DATE / TIME / DATETIME : Temporal types in ISO-8601 format. Temporal Validation Flags : Can be used directly or inside MANDATORY : AFTER : Value must be chronologically after this (e.g., "2020-01-01" , "now" ). BEFORE : Value must be chronologically before this. REQUIRE_OFFSET : (For DATETIME only) If true , requires the presence of a time zone offset (e.g., +05:00 or Z ). 2.3.3.4 Internationalization (I18N) ¶ The DESCRIPTION property can be a plain string or a key in a Resource Bundle. - mConfig looks for Resource Bundles named messages in the same locations as schemas (e.g., .config/messages.properties ). - If a matching key is found in the bundle for the current locale (configured via ConfigFeature.PREFERRED_LANGUAGE ), the localized string is used. - Otherwise, the raw DESCRIPTION string is used as a fallback. 2.3.4 ConfigSchemaFactory ¶ For 1.0 and better multi-language support (JNI/Rust/Python), use ConfigSchemaFactory to create schemas and entries programmatically: ConfigSchemaFactory factory = ConfigSchemaFactory.create(); ConfigSchema schema = factory.createSchema(); ConfigSchemaEntry entry = factory.createEntry("port", ConfigEntryType.NUMBER) .setValidationPattern("uint16") .setDefault("8080"); schema.addSchemaEntry(entry); 2.3.5 Future-Proofing with the MANDATORY block ¶ To ensure that future extensions to the schema format do not break older versions of the library, or conversely, that newer schemas can demand features that older versions must respect, mConfig uses a MANDATORY sub-item. If a schema entry contains a MANDATORY block, the library MUST understand all keys within that block. If any key inside MANDATORY is unknown to the current version of mConfig, the schema loading will fail with an UNKNOWN_MANDATORY_FEATURE error. Example: { "KEY": "network/timeout", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "MANDATORY": { "UNIT": "milliseconds" } } In this example, if a future version of mConfig introduces a UNIT feature and it's placed inside MANDATORY , an older version that doesn't know about UNIT will refuse to load the schema, preventing potential misconfiguration (e.g., interpreting milliseconds as seconds). Features outside the MANDATORY block that are unknown to the library are silently ignored. 2.3.6 Formats ¶ mConfig supports several JSON structures for defining schemas: 2.3.6.1 Named Schema Object ¶ { "my-app-config": { "NAME": "my-app-config", "ENTRIES": [ { "KEY": "port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080 } ] } } 2.3.6.2 List of Entries (Anonymous Schema) ¶ If a JSON file contains only a list of entries, it is treated as a schema for the configuration matching the filename (excluding .mconfig-schema.json ). [ { "KEY": "port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080 } ] 2.3.7 Discovery ¶ Schemas are automatically discovered from multiple locations: Classpath : Scanned within .config/ directories. Filenames should follow the pattern name.mconfig-schema.json . Filesystem (Local Repository) : Scanned in prioritized OS-specific locations to allow system-wide sharing and hardening. Schemas are stored under an app-scoped subdirectory: [<company>/]<application>/<configName>.mconfig-schema.json If company is blank/null/whitespace, the company segment is omitted (app-only paths). Windows : %APPDATA%\mconfig\schemas , %PROGRAMDATA%\mconfig\schemas . Unix/Linux/Mac : ~/.config/mconfig/schemas , /etc/mconfig/schemas , /usr/local/share/mconfig/schemas . Manual : Provided via ConfigFactoryBuilder.setSchemas() . 2.3.7.1 Precedence and Control ¶ By default, schemas found in the filesystem take precedence over those found on the classpath. This allows administrators to override or harden configuration contracts without modifying the application binaries. This behavior can be controlled via ConfigFeature : * ALLOW_LOCAL_SCHEMA_OVERRIDE (default true ): Set to false to ignore filesystem schemas and lock the application to bundled contracts. Deprecated since 0.8.17: 0.9.0 replaces it with an allowlist of schema sources. It keeps working in 0.8.x; keep using it until then. * LOCAL_SCHEMA_DIRECTORY : Can be used to specify a custom directory for schema discovery instead of the OS defaults. Developer Notes ¶ For internals/parsing/validation details, see project devdocs/config_schemas_internals.md (not included in public docs).
docs.title: 2.3 Configuration Schemas

docs.text: Configuration schemas define the contract for a set of configuration entries. They specify what keys are expected, their data types, default values, validation rules, and other metadata.
docs.title: 2.3 Configuration Schemas

docs.text: A schema ensures that the configuration data used by the application is valid and consistent. When a configuration is loaded (e.g., via getConfig(name) ), mConfig attempts to bind it to a matching schema.
docs.title: 2.3.1 Overview

docs.text: Validation : Automatically check if values match expected types and patterns. Defaults : Provide fallback values if none are found in any configuration layer. Documentation : Automatically generate documentation for configuration entries. Type Safety : Preserve data types (e.g., Integer, Boolean) throughout the configuration stack. Security : Identify which entries contain sensitive data (secrets).
docs.title: 2.3.1.1 Benefits of using Schemas

docs.text: Minimal example (single schema entry with a default): [ { "KEY": "server/port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080, "DESCRIPTION": "Listening port" } ] Named schema example (multiple entries): { "my-app-config": { "NAME": "my-app-config", "ENTRIES": [ { "KEY": "server/host", "TYPE": "STRING", "DEFAULT": "127.0.0.1" }, { "KEY": "server/port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080 } ] } }
docs.title: 2.3.2 Example

docs.text: Schemas are typically defined in JSON format. A schema file can contain a single schema or multiple named schemas.
docs.title: 2.3.3 Schema Structure

docs.text: Each entry in a schema (within the ENTRIES list) can have the following properties: Property Type Description KEY String The hierarchical path of the entry (e.g., database/host ). TYPE String The data type: STRING , NUMBER , BOOLEAN , BYTES , MULTIPLE_STRINGS , ENUM , ENUM_SET , URI , FILEPATH , DATE , TIME , DATETIME . DESCRIPTION String Human-readable description or Resource Bundle key for localized description. (Optional) DEFAULT (any) The default value used if no other value is provided. (Optional) PATTERN String A validation pattern (Regex, range specification, or enum list). (Optional) SECRET Boolean If true , the entry holds a cryptographic secret or credential: it is redacted in logs, kept out of the JVM String pool, and retrieved via getSecret() . (Optional, defaults to false ) SENSITIVE Boolean If true , the entry holds information that must not be disclosed, typically personal data under GDPR. Defined but not yet enforced — see below. (Optional, defaults to false ) HIDDEN Boolean If true , the entry is hidden from automatic documentation. (Optional, defaults to false ) FLAGS Array Declarative markers for the entry: MANDATORY , READ_ONLY , WRITE_ONLY , SECRET , SENSITIVE . Not all are enforced yet — see below. ARITY String The number of allowed occurrences (e.g., 1 , 0..1 , 1..* ). (Optional; see defaults below) MANDATORY Object (Optional) Block for future-proofing and strict requirements. Note this is the block , distinct from the MANDATORY entry in FLAGS . See below. AFTER String (Optional) For temporal types, value must be after this (ISO format or now ). BEFORE String (Optional) For temporal types, value must be before this (ISO format or now ). REQUIRE_OFFSET Boolean (Optional) For DATETIME , requires an offset (e.g., +02:00 or Z ). Property names are matched case-insensitively, so "KEY" and "key" are equivalent.
docs.title: 2.3.3.1 Schema Entry Properties

docs.text: An entry of TYPE BOOLEAN accepts true/false , yes/no , on/off and 1/0 , in any case and with surrounding blanks; a DEFAULT of "on" is valid. Any other value, an empty one included, does not match the schema. Such a value is skipped when read: the next layer, or finally the DEFAULT , applies, so a typing error in one file does not switch a feature off. Writing such a value through put() is rejected. (Up to 0.8.16 the check accepted true and false only.) Without a schema, getBoolean() uses the first value found and throws ConfigException ( CONVERSION_FAILURE ) if it is not one of these literals. See LENIENT_BOOLEAN_CONVERSION for the plain Java behaviour.
docs.title: Boolean values

docs.text: These mark two different kinds of confidentiality, and most entries that are SECRET are also SENSITIVE — though rarely the reverse. In short: SECRET is for cryptographic secrets and passwords, SENSITIVE for information that must not leak into view, such as personal data. See Secret and Sensitive for the full model, including which storage places will accept which kind of data. Both markers suppress disclosure of the value only. The storage location of a marked entry stays traceable through getScope() , getLocation() and getURI() , so protected data remains findable, correctable and erasable.
docs.title: Confidentiality markers: SECRET and SENSITIVE

docs.text: The FLAGS array is accepted and parsed, but the library does not yet act on every marker in it: Marker Enforced? Notes MANDATORY yes via FLAGS ; drives default arity and presence validation SECRET yes only via the SECRET property , not via FLAGS (see the warning below) SENSITIVE no recognised and stored; no redaction or export suppression yet READ_ONLY no recognised and stored; writes are not blocked yet WRITE_ONLY no recognised and stored; reads are not blocked yet Warning: "FLAGS": ["SECRET"] does not currently mark an entry as secret. The flag is stored but is not consulted by the secrets handling, which reads only the separate SECRET property. Always write "SECRET": true . Using the flag alone means the value is not protected — no redaction, no SecretValue , no wiping. Since 0.8.15, loading a schema logs a WARNING for each entry that uses a marker without effect: SECRET in FLAGS without "SECRET": true (the value is not protected), and SENSITIVE , READ_ONLY or WRITE_ONLY (not enforced yet). SECRET in FLAGS next to "SECRET": true is redundant and not reported. 0.9.0 will be stricter.
docs.title: Which markers are enforced today

docs.text: The ARITY property defines the constraints on the number of elements for an entry. This is especially useful for MULTIPLE_STRINGS and ENUM_SET types. Exact number : "ARITY": "3" (exactly 3 items required). Range : "ARITY": "1..5" (minimum 1, maximum 5 items). Open-ended : "ARITY": "1..*" or "ARITY": "1..n" (at least 1 item, no upper limit). Defaults : Mandatory entries: 1 Optional entries: 0..1 List types ( MULTIPLE_STRINGS , ENUM_SET ): 0..* (optional) or 1..* (mandatory).
docs.title: 2.3.3.2 Arity (ARITY)

docs.text: Validation patterns depend on the TYPE of the entry: STRING : A Java Regular Expression. Compiled with Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS by default, supporting Unicode property escapes like \p{L} . NUMBER : Mathematical Interval Notation : Supports [min, max] , (min, max) , [min, max) , and (min, max] . Example: [1024, 65535] . Predefined Aliases : Unsigned: uint8 (0-255), uint16 , uint32 , uint64 . Signed: int8 (-128 to 127), int16 , int32 , int64 , and custom bit-widths like int7 , int15 , int31 , int63 . ENUM / ENUM_SET : A pipe-separated list of valid options. Example: DEBUG|INFO|WARN|ERROR . URI : A valid URI string (RFC 3986). FILEPATH : A valid path on the filesystem. Path Validation Flags : Can be placed inside the MANDATORY block for semantic checks: EXISTS : true (path must exist) IS_DIRECTORY : true (path must be a directory) IS_FILE : true (path must be a regular file) CAN_WRITE : true (path must be writable) DATE / TIME / DATETIME : Temporal types in ISO-8601 format. Temporal Validation Flags : Can be used directly or inside MANDATORY : AFTER : Value must be chronologically after this (e.g., "2020-01-01" , "now" ). BEFORE : Value must be chronologically before this. REQUIRE_OFFSET : (For DATETIME only) If true , requires the presence of a time zone offset (e.g., +05:00 or Z ).
docs.title: 2.3.3.3 Validation Patterns (PATTERN)

docs.text: The DESCRIPTION property can be a plain string or a key in a Resource Bundle. - mConfig looks for Resource Bundles named messages in the same locations as schemas (e.g., .config/messages.properties ). - If a matching key is found in the bundle for the current locale (configured via ConfigFeature.PREFERRED_LANGUAGE ), the localized string is used. - Otherwise, the raw DESCRIPTION string is used as a fallback.
docs.title: 2.3.3.4 Internationalization (I18N)

docs.text: For 1.0 and better multi-language support (JNI/Rust/Python), use ConfigSchemaFactory to create schemas and entries programmatically: ConfigSchemaFactory factory = ConfigSchemaFactory.create(); ConfigSchema schema = factory.createSchema(); ConfigSchemaEntry entry = factory.createEntry("port", ConfigEntryType.NUMBER) .setValidationPattern("uint16") .setDefault("8080"); schema.addSchemaEntry(entry);
docs.title: 2.3.4 ConfigSchemaFactory

docs.text: To ensure that future extensions to the schema format do not break older versions of the library, or conversely, that newer schemas can demand features that older versions must respect, mConfig uses a MANDATORY sub-item. If a schema entry contains a MANDATORY block, the library MUST understand all keys within that block. If any key inside MANDATORY is unknown to the current version of mConfig, the schema loading will fail with an UNKNOWN_MANDATORY_FEATURE error. Example: { "KEY": "network/timeout", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "MANDATORY": { "UNIT": "milliseconds" } } In this example, if a future version of mConfig introduces a UNIT feature and it's placed inside MANDATORY , an older version that doesn't know about UNIT will refuse to load the schema, preventing potential misconfiguration (e.g., interpreting milliseconds as seconds). Features outside the MANDATORY block that are unknown to the library are silently ignored.
docs.title: 2.3.5 Future-Proofing with the MANDATORY block

docs.text: mConfig supports several JSON structures for defining schemas:
docs.title: 2.3.6 Formats

docs.text: { "my-app-config": { "NAME": "my-app-config", "ENTRIES": [ { "KEY": "port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080 } ] } }
docs.title: 2.3.6.1 Named Schema Object

docs.text: If a JSON file contains only a list of entries, it is treated as a schema for the configuration matching the filename (excluding .mconfig-schema.json ). [ { "KEY": "port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080 } ]
docs.title: 2.3.6.2 List of Entries (Anonymous Schema)

docs.text: Schemas are automatically discovered from multiple locations: Classpath : Scanned within .config/ directories. Filenames should follow the pattern name.mconfig-schema.json . Filesystem (Local Repository) : Scanned in prioritized OS-specific locations to allow system-wide sharing and hardening. Schemas are stored under an app-scoped subdirectory: [<company>/]<application>/<configName>.mconfig-schema.json If company is blank/null/whitespace, the company segment is omitted (app-only paths). Windows : %APPDATA%\mconfig\schemas , %PROGRAMDATA%\mconfig\schemas . Unix/Linux/Mac : ~/.config/mconfig/schemas , /etc/mconfig/schemas , /usr/local/share/mconfig/schemas . Manual : Provided via ConfigFactoryBuilder.setSchemas() .
docs.title: 2.3.7 Discovery

docs.text: By default, schemas found in the filesystem take precedence over those found on the classpath. This allows administrators to override or harden configuration contracts without modifying the application binaries. This behavior can be controlled via ConfigFeature : * ALLOW_LOCAL_SCHEMA_OVERRIDE (default true ): Set to false to ignore filesystem schemas and lock the application to bundled contracts. Deprecated since 0.8.17: 0.9.0 replaces it with an allowlist of schema sources. It keeps working in 0.8.x; keep using it until then. * LOCAL_SCHEMA_DIRECTORY : Can be used to specify a custom directory for schema discovery instead of the OS defaults.
docs.title: 2.3.7.1 Precedence and Control

docs.text: For internals/parsing/validation details, see project devdocs/config_schemas_internals.md (not included in public docs).
docs.title: Developer Notes

docs.text: 2.4 Comment Handling in mConfig ¶ Of the possible configuration sources, files are the ones that support comments. Comments in configuration files are an important source of information for users. They can be used to explain configuration options, document decisions, provide context, or include relevant links. mConfig aims to keep comments intact in configuration files to ensure that human-readable information is not lost during programmatic updates. Core Principles ¶ Write-Preservation : Writing to a configuration file should not erase existing comments. Read-Write Symmetry : Maintaining the original structure and documentation of the file is a priority. Human-Centric : Comments are for humans. They should not be used for machine processing or "shebang" style logic. Programmatic Comments ¶ While mConfig prioritizes preserving existing comments, it also supports adding comments programmatically: Description from Schema : When an entry is first created, mConfig can automatically include the description defined in the ConfigSchema as a comment. This is controlled by the ConfigFeature.DESCRIPTION_ON_CREATE feature. Explicit Comments : Developers can add comments to a ConfigEntry using the setComment(String) method. This is useful for documenting automated changes (e.g., "# AUTO-REDUCED: Disk space was below 5%"). Configuration Features ¶ The behavior of comment handling is governed by several ConfigFeature flags: ConfigFeature.COMMENTS_WRITING (default: false ): When set to true , mConfig will write programmatic comments to the configuration. Even when false , the library still attempts to preserve existing comments for supported formats. ConfigFeature.COMMENTS_READING (default: false ): Enables reading comments from files into the ConfigEntry objects. Note that determining exactly which lines belong to which key is heuristic-based and may not be perfect for all formats. ConfigFeature.DESCRIPTION_ON_CREATE (default: false ): When true , uses the description field from the ConfigSchemaEntry to populate comments for new entries. Format Support Matrix ¶ Preservation of comments depends on the underlying format module. Some high-level libraries (like Jackson) may strip comments by design. File Format mConfig Module Preserve Comments .properties mConfigFormatJavaProperties Yes INI mConfigFormatINI Yes TOML mConfigFormatTOML Yes YAML mConfigFormatYAMLwithSnakeYAML Partially TOML mConfigFormatTOMLwithJackson No YAML mConfigFormatYAMLwithJackson No JSON mConfigFormatJSONwithJackson No JSON5 mConfigFormatJSONwithJackson No Implementation Details ¶ Multi-line Comments ¶ Representation : Represented as a single String with \n line separators. Markers : On reading, format-specific markers (e.g., # , ! , ; ) are preserved. Writing : mConfig ensures each line is correctly prefixed with the format's primary marker if it's missing. Heuristics and Association ¶ Leading Comments : Consecutive comment lines immediately preceding a key are associated with that key. Global Headers : Comment blocks at the top of a file (or between entries) separated by empty lines are treated as "Global Headers". They are preserved and rewritten at the top of the file but are not attached to any specific ConfigEntry . Inline Comments : Comments on the same line as a value are appended to the entry's comment string on a best-effort basis. Priority and Merging ¶ When writing an entry, comments are merged based on the following priority (top to bottom): 1. Description from Schema : If DESCRIPTION_ON_CREATE=true and the entry is new. 2. Existing Comments : Preserved from the original file. 3. Programmatic Comments : Added via ConfigEntry.setComment() . Duplicate lines are automatically filtered during the merge process.
docs.title: 2.4 Comment Handling

docs.text: 2.5 Config Features ¶ ConfigFeature flags tune how a ConfigFactory is built and how it behaves. Set them on the ConfigFactoryBuilder before calling build() . mConfig uses a two-tier system for features: 1. Core Features : Standard settings defined in the ConfigFeature enum (e.g., TEST_MODE , LOGLEVEL_NUMBER ). 2. Extension Features : Module-specific settings (e.g., VaultFeatures.BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME ) that are automatically registered when the module is on the classpath. Example using both: ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "ourApp") // Core features (using enum) .setFeature(ConfigFeature.ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS, true) .setFeature(ConfigFeature.EXCEPTION_ON_MISSING_ENTRY, false) // Extension feature (using module-specific class) .setFeature(VaultFeatures.BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME, "custom-vault"); Config Feature Registry ¶ mConfig maintains a central ConfigFeatureRegistry that handles all features case-insensitively. This allows you to set features using their string names, which is particularly useful if you want to avoid a compile-time dependency on a specific extension module: // Using a string key for a core feature builder.setFeature("ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS", true); // Using a string key for an extension feature builder.setFeature("VAULT_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME", "custom-vault"); If a feature is not yet registered (e.g., because the module hasn't been initialized), the value is stored as a raw property and validated once the module attempts to access it. Notes: - Booleans default to false unless a default is explicitly listed below. - Extension features are only available when the corresponding module is on the classpath. - Runtime environment variables can override a subset of settings if ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS is enabled. See "Runtime overrides" below. - Security-relevant features can only be set in code, or by the component itself. See "Who may set a feature" below. Self-configuration per component ¶ An application often contains several components that use mConfig, each building its own ConfigFactory with its own company and application name. Each component can ship its own settings as a classpath resource: src/main/resources/.config/<company>/<application>/mconfig.properties (without a company name: .config/<application>/mconfig.properties ). Keys are feature names, values are strings; lists are comma-separated: COMMENTS_READING=true FILE_FORMAT_READING_PRIORITIES=YAML,properties The file applies only to factories created with that company and application name, so a component configures itself without changing the behaviour of the other components or of the main application. Precedence, highest first: code ( setFeature() ), runtime settings (if delegated, see below), the component file , the deprecated global file . A file only fills in features that are not set yet. Self-configuration is read during build() , before the test-mode gates are evaluated. Switch it off with ConfigFeature.ENABLE_SELF_CONFIGURATION=false (in code). Deprecated: the global file .config/metabit/mConfig/mconfig.properties . It applies to every factory in the process and cannot be attributed to a component; arbitrary resources on the classpath may come from any dependency. It is still read in 0.8.x, with a WARNING naming its location, may only set ordinary features (level ANY ), and will be removed before 0.9.0 . Move its settings to the component file. Who may set a feature ¶ Features reach the ConfigFactory through these channels: Channel How Who decides Code ConfigFactoryBuilder.setFeature() the component (or application) Delegated runtime settings: MCONFIG_RUNTIME_* environment variables, -Dmconfig.runtime.* system properties whoever starts the process, after the component enabled ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS in code Component file .config/<company>/<application>/mconfig.properties on the classpath the component's author Global file (deprecated) .config/metabit/mConfig/mconfig.properties on the classpath any JAR or directory on the classpath Each feature has a setting level ( ConfigFeatureInterface.getSettingLevel() ) that says which channels may set it: Level Code Delegated Component file Global file CODE_ONLY yes no no no COMPONENT yes yes yes no ANY yes yes yes yes A channel that may not set a feature ignores the value and logs a WARNING. Most features are ANY ; module-specific features are ANY unless the module says otherwise. The restricted ones: Feature Level Why ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS CODE_ONLY it is the delegation to the environment; that is a decision for code ENABLE_SELF_CONFIGURATION CODE_ONLY a file cannot decide whether files are read ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS CODE_ONLY see POLICY locations ADDITIONAL_MODULE_PATHS CODE_ONLY it loads code TEST_MODE COMPONENT each component is responsible for its own test mode TESTMODE_DIRECTORIES COMPONENT belongs to test mode PERMIT_TEST_MODE COMPONENT belongs to test mode; code wins, so a file cannot undo a lockdown set in code ALLOW_INCOMPLETE_SERVICE_REGISTRATION COMPONENT a component accepts its own packaging fault, not every component's LOG_PARSE_ERROR_DETAILS CODE_ONLY may put secret values into the log; an explicit decision of the developer LENIENT_BOOLEAN_CONVERSION COMPONENT how a component reads its own files, not every component's Why "delegated" is different from a classpath file. Runtime settings only work after the component enabled them in code, so it has explicitly handed these decisions to whoever starts the process (a CI pipeline, an operator). That is why a file can never enable them. Test mode and the main application. Each component is responsible for its own testing and test mode; it may switch test mode on in code, through runtime settings, or in its own file. A component file that requests test mode is logged as a WARNING with the file's location, so an accidentally shipped file is visible at once. The main application keeps control over all components: ConfigFactoryBuilder.forbidTestMode() locks test mode off for the whole JVM, and PERMIT_TEST_MODE=false per factory (see Test Mode ). Runtime overrides ¶ If ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS is set to true in code, mConfig accepts runtime settings via environment variables with the prefix MCONFIG_RUNTIME_ , and via system properties ( -Dmconfig.runtime.test_mode=true , or verbatim -DMCONFIG_RUNTIME_TEST_MODE=true ; the system property wins): MCONFIG_RUNTIME_DEBUG_LEVEL -> LOGLEVEL_NUMBER (accepts numbers or: off , error , warn , info , debug , trace ) MCONFIG_RUNTIME_DEBUG_OUTPUT -> LOGGING_REDIRECT_TARGET MCONFIG_RUNTIME_DISABLE_MODULES -> DISABLED_MODULE_IDS (comma-separated) MCONFIG_RUNTIME_TEST_MODE -> TEST_MODE MCONFIG_RUNTIME_KUBERNETES_* -> Kubernetes module paths and endpoint (see the module README) MCONFIG_RUNTIME_MODULES -> ADDITIONAL_MODULE_PATHS : refused since 0.8.15, as the feature is CODE_ONLY . POLICY locations registered by the application ¶ POLICY is meant for administrator-controlled locations, which the storages derive from the operating system (e.g. /etc/... , the Windows registry policy keys). In productive mode, mConfig refuses POLICY locations that the application registers itself, with a ConfigException ( ARGUMENT_REFUSED ) at build() : a POLICY: prefix in ADDITIONAL_RUNTIME_DIRECTORIES or ADDITIONAL_USER_DIRECTORIES ; a secrets provider in ADDITIONAL_SECRETS_PROVIDERS with "scope": "POLICY" ; a POLICY-scope source added with ConfigFactoryBuilder.addSource() . They are allowed in test mode, and with ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS set in code, for applications that legitimately ship their own policy location (e.g. administration tools). Feature reference ¶ Test mode ¶ PERMIT_TEST_MODE (Boolean, default: true; level COMPONENT ): Master gate for test mode usage. TEST_MODE (Boolean, default: false; level COMPONENT ): Activate test-mode search locations. TESTMODE_DIRECTORIES ( List<String> , default: empty; level COMPONENT ): Scoped paths in SCOPE:PATH format. TESTMODE_PARAMETERS ( Map<String,String> ): Additional test parameters. Logging ¶ QUIET (Boolean, default: false): Reduce internal mConfig logging. LOGGING_TO_USE_IN_CONFIGLIB (String, default: ""): Force a specific logging module. LOGLEVEL_NUMBER (Integer, default: 4): Numeric log level for basic loggers. LOGGING_REDIRECT_TARGET (String): Redirect internal logging ( stderr , stdout , quiet , file:<path> ). Filesystem and registry paths ¶ ADDITIONAL_RUNTIME_DIRECTORIES ( List<String> ): Extra filesystem directories (prepended) for RUNTIME scope. ADDITIONAL_USER_DIRECTORIES ( List<String> ): Extra filesystem directories (prepended) for USER scope. Entries of both may carry a scope prefix ( HOST:/opt/app/conf ); POLICY: needs ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS in productive mode (see POLICY locations ). FILENAME_EXTENSION_MAPPINGS ( List<String> ): Extra filename extensions to try when reading config files. DEFAULT_TEXTFILE_CHARSET ( String , default: UTF-8 ): Charset for text formats. TRIM_TEXTVALUE_SPACES (Boolean, default: true): Trim leading/trailing spaces in text values. LENIENT_BOOLEAN_CONVERSION (Boolean, default: false; component; since 0.8.17): Read Boolean values as Boolean.parseBoolean() does: true in any case is true, every other value, typing errors included, is false. By default getBoolean() accepts true/false , yes/no , on/off and 1/0 (any case, surrounding blanks) and throws ConfigException ( CONVERSION_FAILURE ) for anything else, an empty value included. For compatibility with files written for the plain Java behaviour. Limitation: it acts in the Configuration getters only. Code that converts a ConfigEntry itself ( getValueAsBoolean() ), the ConfigMapper, and the schema check of BOOLEAN entries always convert strictly. Boolean features themselves (in mconfig.properties , setTestParameters() ) are always read strictly as well. WRITE_CONDENSED_FORMAT (Boolean, default: false): Prefer compact output when writing text formats. Format priorities ¶ FILE_FORMAT_READING_PRIORITIES ( List<String> , default: DHALL,TOML,YAML,JSON5,JSON,ASN1,properties,INI ): Read order. FILE_FORMAT_WRITING_PRIORITIES ( List<String> , default: TOML,YAML,JSON5,JSON,properties ): Write order. FILE_FORMAT_READING_ALLOW_ALL_FORMATS (Boolean, default: true): Fallback to non-listed formats. FILE_FORMAT_WRITING_ALLOW_ALL_FORMATS (Boolean, default: true): Fallback to non-listed formats. Storage type priorities ¶ STORAGE_TYPE_PRIORITIES ( List<String> , default: RAM,secrets,vault,aws-secrets,files,registry,registryjni,zookeeper,JAR ): Init/search order within a scope. STORAGE_TYPE_ALLOW_ALL_STORAGES (Boolean, default: true): Allow storages not explicitly listed. Set to false to use only the storages covered by STORAGE_TYPE_PRIORITIES ; the others are not initialised and read nothing. An entry covers the storage ID itself and the IDs it prefixes up to a - or . ( RAM covers RAM-RUNTIME and RAM-SESSION , secrets covers secrets.<provider> ). Core's own storages ( defaults , RAM-* ) are always used. Storages missing from the default list, such as envvar (environment variables) or kubernetes , must be added explicitly. Sources added with addSource() are not affected. The INFO line at factory start lists the storages in use. Schemas and defaults ¶ CONFIG_SCHEMA_LIST ( Map<String,ConfigSchema> ): Provide schemas programmatically. SCHEMA_STRICT_MODE (Boolean, default: false): Reject keys not in the schema. SCHEMA_RESETS_DEFAULTS (Boolean, default: false): Replace existing defaults instead of merging. Configurations without a schema are allowed by default; there is no feature flag to switch that on. Set SCHEMA_STRICT_MODE to true if you want unschemad keys rejected instead. Missing entry behavior ¶ EXCEPTION_ON_MISSING_ENTRY (Boolean, default: true): Throw when a key is absent. DEFAULT_ON_MISSING_ENTRY (Boolean): deprecated since 0.8.17, never evaluated, removed in 0.9.0. Schema DEFAULT values apply anyway; with EXCEPTION_ON_MISSING_ENTRY=false , a key with neither value nor default returns null . EXCEPTION_WHEN_CONFIGURATION_NOT_FOUND (Boolean, default: false): Throw if a configuration name is not found at all. FALLBACKS_ACROSS_SCOPES (Boolean, default: true): Allow fallback to less specific scopes on reads. (Available via ZooKeeperFeatures in mConfigSourceZooKeeper ) Vault (mConfigSourceVault) ¶ VAULT_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME (String, default: vault ): Bootstrap config name. (Available via VaultFeatures in mConfigSourceVault ) AWS Secrets Manager (mConfigSourceAwsSecretsManager) ¶ AWS_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME (String, default: aws ): Bootstrap config name. docs.title: 2.5 Config Features

docs.text: ConfigFeature flags tune how a ConfigFactory is built and how it behaves. Set them on the ConfigFactoryBuilder before calling build() . mConfig uses a two-tier system for features: 1. Core Features : Standard settings defined in the ConfigFeature enum (e.g., TEST_MODE , LOGLEVEL_NUMBER ). 2. Extension Features : Module-specific settings (e.g., VaultFeatures.BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME ) that are automatically registered when the module is on the classpath. Example using both: ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "ourApp") // Core features (using enum) .setFeature(ConfigFeature.ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS, true) .setFeature(ConfigFeature.EXCEPTION_ON_MISSING_ENTRY, false) // Extension feature (using module-specific class) .setFeature(VaultFeatures.BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME, "custom-vault");
docs.title: 2.5 Config Features

docs.text: mConfig maintains a central ConfigFeatureRegistry that handles all features case-insensitively. This allows you to set features using their string names, which is particularly useful if you want to avoid a compile-time dependency on a specific extension module: // Using a string key for a core feature builder.setFeature("ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS", true); // Using a string key for an extension feature builder.setFeature("VAULT_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_NAME", "custom-vault"); If a feature is not yet registered (e.g., because the module hasn't been initialized), the value is stored as a raw property and validated once the module attempts to access it. Notes: - Booleans default to false unless a default is explicitly listed below. - Extension features are only available when the corresponding module is on the classpath. - Runtime environment variables can override a subset of settings if ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS is enabled. See "Runtime overrides" below. - Security-relevant features can only be set in code, or by the component itself. See "Who may set a feature" below.
docs.title: Config Feature Registry

docs.text: An application often contains several components that use mConfig, each building its own ConfigFactory with its own company and application name. Each component can ship its own settings as a classpath resource: src/main/resources/.config/<company>/<application>/mconfig.properties (without a company name: .config/<application>/mconfig.properties ). Keys are feature names, values are strings; lists are comma-separated: COMMENTS_READING=true FILE_FORMAT_READING_PRIORITIES=YAML,properties The file applies only to factories created with that company and application name, so a component configures itself without changing the behaviour of the other components or of the main application. Precedence, highest first: code ( setFeature() ), runtime settings (if delegated, see below), the component file , the deprecated global file . A file only fills in features that are not set yet. Self-configuration is read during build() , before the test-mode gates are evaluated. Switch it off with ConfigFeature.ENABLE_SELF_CONFIGURATION=false (in code). Deprecated: the global file .config/metabit/mConfig/mconfig.properties . It applies to every factory in the process and cannot be attributed to a component; arbitrary resources on the classpath may come from any dependency. It is still read in 0.8.x, with a WARNING naming its location, may only set ordinary features (level ANY ), and will be removed before 0.9.0 . Move its settings to the component file.
docs.title: Self-configuration per component

docs.text: Features reach the ConfigFactory through these channels: Channel How Who decides Code ConfigFactoryBuilder.setFeature() the component (or application) Delegated runtime settings: MCONFIG_RUNTIME_* environment variables, -Dmconfig.runtime.* system properties whoever starts the process, after the component enabled ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS in code Component file .config/<company>/<application>/mconfig.properties on the classpath the component's author Global file (deprecated) .config/metabit/mConfig/mconfig.properties on the classpath any JAR or directory on the classpath Each feature has a setting level ( ConfigFeatureInterface.getSettingLevel() ) that says which channels may set it: Level Code Delegated Component file Global file CODE_ONLY yes no no no COMPONENT yes yes yes no ANY yes yes yes yes A channel that may not set a feature ignores the value and logs a WARNING. Most features are ANY ; module-specific features are ANY unless the module says otherwise. The restricted ones: Feature Level Why ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS CODE_ONLY it is the delegation to the environment; that is a decision for code ENABLE_SELF_CONFIGURATION CODE_ONLY a file cannot decide whether files are read ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS CODE_ONLY see POLICY locations ADDITIONAL_MODULE_PATHS CODE_ONLY it loads code TEST_MODE COMPONENT each component is responsible for its own test mode TESTMODE_DIRECTORIES COMPONENT belongs to test mode PERMIT_TEST_MODE COMPONENT belongs to test mode; code wins, so a file cannot undo a lockdown set in code ALLOW_INCOMPLETE_SERVICE_REGISTRATION COMPONENT a component accepts its own packaging fault, not every component's LOG_PARSE_ERROR_DETAILS CODE_ONLY may put secret values into the log; an explicit decision of the developer LENIENT_BOOLEAN_CONVERSION COMPONENT how a component reads its own files, not every component's Why "delegated" is different from a classpath file. Runtime settings only work after the component enabled them in code, so it has explicitly handed these decisions to whoever starts the process (a CI pipeline, an operator). That is why a file can never enable them. Test mode and the main application. Each component is responsible for its own testing and test mode; it may switch test mode on in code, through runtime settings, or in its own file. A component file that requests test mode is logged as a WARNING with the file's location, so an accidentally shipped file is visible at once. The main application keeps control over all components: ConfigFactoryBuilder.forbidTestMode() locks test mode off for the whole JVM, and PERMIT_TEST_MODE=false per factory (see Test Mode ).
docs.title: Who may set a feature

docs.text: If ALLOW_MCONFIG_RUNTIME_SETTINGS is set to true in code, mConfig accepts runtime settings via environment variables with the prefix MCONFIG_RUNTIME_ , and via system properties ( -Dmconfig.runtime.test_mode=true , or verbatim -DMCONFIG_RUNTIME_TEST_MODE=true ; the system property wins): MCONFIG_RUNTIME_DEBUG_LEVEL -> LOGLEVEL_NUMBER (accepts numbers or: off , error , warn , info , debug , trace ) MCONFIG_RUNTIME_DEBUG_OUTPUT -> LOGGING_REDIRECT_TARGET MCONFIG_RUNTIME_DISABLE_MODULES -> DISABLED_MODULE_IDS (comma-separated) MCONFIG_RUNTIME_TEST_MODE -> TEST_MODE MCONFIG_RUNTIME_KUBERNETES_* -> Kubernetes module paths and endpoint (see the module README) MCONFIG_RUNTIME_MODULES -> ADDITIONAL_MODULE_PATHS : refused since 0.8.15, as the feature is CODE_ONLY .
docs.title: Runtime overrides

docs.text: POLICY is meant for administrator-controlled locations, which the storages derive from the operating system (e.g. /etc/... , the Windows registry policy keys). In productive mode, mConfig refuses POLICY locations that the application registers itself, with a ConfigException ( ARGUMENT_REFUSED ) at build() : a POLICY: prefix in ADDITIONAL_RUNTIME_DIRECTORIES or ADDITIONAL_USER_DIRECTORIES ; a secrets provider in ADDITIONAL_SECRETS_PROVIDERS with "scope": "POLICY" ; a POLICY-scope source added with ConfigFactoryBuilder.addSource() . They are allowed in test mode, and with ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS set in code, for applications that legitimately ship their own policy location (e.g. administration tools).

docs.text: Security Model ¶ The mConfig modules function as a library, running within the application’s context and process environment. mConfig operates with the application's inherent access rights and does not attempt to "guard" secrets from the application itself. Instead, it delegates the primary security boundary to the underlying execution environment (e.g., OS, Kubernetes, or Cloud IAM roles), maintaining the same level of security as the host process. What mConfig protects against, and what not ¶ mConfig prevents accidental disclosure of secret values: in logs, toString() , tool output, exports and diagnostic dumps (see Where secret values may appear ). mConfig does not protect secrets in process memory . Whoever can read the memory of the process - a heap dump, a debugger, an agent attached to the JVM, other code running in the same process, the operating-system user the process runs as - can read the secrets the application has loaded. Erasing (see Memory wiping ) shortens the time a value is held, which limits what a later heap dump contains; it is no protection against an attacker with access to the running process. Protecting secrets from the process itself takes handles instead of values, such as keys kept in an HSM or a KMS. Secrets ¶ Bridging Modern and Legacy security ¶ Ideally, an application never handles raw secrets, but operates via handles only. This is the model of the JCE (Java Cryptography Extension) and of Hardware Security Modules (HSMs): keys stay in a hardware enclave and are used in a controlled manner, without ever entering application memory. Many common tasks, however - sending a bearer token to an API, a password to a database driver - require the actual secret value. mConfig acts as bridge for both: High Security: Manage IDs and handles for HSM/KMS providers. Practical Utility: fetch and provide plaintext tokens or passwords for legacy interfaces, with the exposure limited as described below. mConfig Secrets Handling ¶ mConfig secrets are treated differently than standard configuration to reduce their exposure footprint: Masking : secret values are replaced by [REDACTED] in logs, toString() and tool output. Transport : the network sources use TLS. The Vault and Kubernetes modules send the Kubernetes ServiceAccount token only to an https address, unless insecure transport is explicitly allowed for development. Other credentials, such as a static Vault token, go to the address you configure: configure an https address. Memory : secret values are handed out as SecretValue , a mutable byte buffer that the application can wipe with erase() , instead of an immutable String . Late-bound decryption : in the configuration, a secret is a reference. It is resolved - fetched, and decrypted where its source keeps it encrypted - only when the application requests the value ( getSecret() ), and the visible bytes can be erased right after use. Status: this is the model the secrets handling is built for. The storages shipped today still fetch their secrets when the configuration is built; fetching on request (lazy fetch) is scheduled for 0.9.1. Strings are immutable and stay on the heap until garbage collected, so a password kept as a String cannot be wiped. A SecretValue can. This works only as far as the value was never a String along the way: values read from text formats ( .properties , JSON, YAML, …) pass through the format parser as String s, and environment variables are String s in the JVM from the start. The buffer reduces the exposure; it does not remove it. Dynamic Updates ¶ Vault and AWS Secrets Manager are polled for changes ( pollInterval ; default 60 s for Vault, 5 min for AWS, where API calls have costs; 0 disables polling). The Kubernetes module watches the ConfigMaps and Secrets it reads. Changed values replace the old ones without a process restart, so rotated credentials are picked up. Memory wiping ¶ When a Configuration is closed via close() , mConfig calls erase() on its configuration layers. The in-memory and default layers and the environment-variable, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and Kubernetes storages wipe the secret buffers they hold. Layers read from files do not wipe yet ; complete wipe-on-close is planned for 0.9.1. With the storages shipped with mConfig, each getSecret() returns a new copy, so wiping it with erase() after use affects only the application's copy, never the stored value. A third-party secrets provider (see Where secrets come from ) should do the same. Secret and Sensitive ¶ mConfig distinguishes two kinds of confidentiality. They are related, but they are protected for different reasons and therefore handled differently. SECRET — cryptographic secrets and credentials: private keys, symmetric keys, API tokens, passwords, license IDs. If one leaks, a system is compromised. SENSITIVE — information that must not become visible where it does not belong, typically personal data under GDPR and comparable regimes: names, e-mail addresses, postal addresses, user IDs, IP addresses. If one leaks, a person is harmed and a reporting obligation may follow. The two overlap: most SECRET entries are also SENSITIVE, but far from every SENSITIVE entry is SECRET. A per-user API token is both a credential and personal data. A customer's e-mail address is personal data and no credential at all. The two markers are therefore independent, not a severity scale — an entry may carry either, both, or neither, and when both are set the protections add up. The distinction in one sentence ¶ SECRET minimises exposure in time . SENSITIVE minimises exposure in scope . A credential is dangerous for as long as it exists in readable form, so mConfig wraps it, keeps it out of the JVM String pool, and wipes it once it is no longer needed. Personal data is not made safe by wiping it — the application legitimately needs it for its normal working life — but it must not spread into logs, exports, diagnostic dumps, or documentation. This is why SENSITIVE deliberately does not use the SecretValue machinery. Forcing personal data through a wipeable byte buffer would be counterproductive: the application would convert it straight back into a String to use it, and nothing would be gained. Confidentiality never hides the location ¶ What gets suppressed is the value . Where the value is stored always remains traceable. mConfig can tell you, for any entry, which scope and which concrete location it came from — getScope() , getLocation() and getURI() on a ConfigEntry answer this regardless of whether the entry is SECRET, SENSITIVE, or neither. That property is deliberate and is kept intact by every confidentiality mechanism in the library. This matters most precisely for the data that is most protected: Data subjects can exercise their rights. Finding, correcting, and erasing personal data (GDPR Art. 15-17) is only possible if one can determine where the data is held. A redaction that also hid the storage location would obstruct the very obligations SENSITIVE exists to serve. Owners keep authority over their data. If a value comes from "somewhere" and its origin cannot be determined, part of the ownership over it is lost. Credentials can be rotated and revoked. Knowing which store holds a secret is a precondition for replacing or removing it. So a redacted log line or diagnostic dump still names the key, the scope, and the storage location of a protected entry — it withholds only the value itself. Location traceability across a ten-tier hierarchy of heterogeneous sources is a distinguishing property of mConfig, and confidentiality markers do not trade it away. Where secret values may appear ¶ Secrets are often stored in plain text on purpose: in a configuration file readable only by the service account, in the registry, in a Kubernetes Secret. Their protection is the access control of that storage — file permissions, ACLs, the login to a network service. mConfig respects this and draws one line: The storage the value came from is the value's home. When a secret is replaced with a new value in the same scope, mConfig writes the new value to the same location, if that location is writeable, and replaces it there. The other secrets stored there stay as they are. Every other context is outside that access control. A newly created file ( ConfigMapper.saveTo() ), console output, logs, diagnostic dumps, event messages: whoever reads these was not necessarily allowed to read the original storage. Secret values do not go there. A storage module may decline to hold SECRET data, and may equally decline to hold SENSITIVE data, on the grounds that this storage place is not safe for the type of information being handled . If no acceptable location exists, the write is refused rather than moved further. The mechanism is the normal write path. A write stays in the scope it was made for and goes through that scope's locations in priority order. A storage declines a location by not offering a writeable layer there, or by not creating one; the write then moves on to the next location of the scope. A storage can also refuse a single entry when it is written - the entry tells whether it is secret. Such a refusal currently ends the write with an error instead of moving on, which is the safe behaviour under the rule above. docs.text: The mConfig modules function as a library, running within the application’s context and process environment. mConfig operates with the application's inherent access rights and does not attempt to "guard" secrets from the application itself. Instead, it delegates the primary security boundary to the underlying execution environment (e.g., OS, Kubernetes, or Cloud IAM roles), maintaining the same level of security as the host process.
docs.title: Security Model

docs.text: mConfig prevents accidental disclosure of secret values: in logs, toString() , tool output, exports and diagnostic dumps (see Where secret values may appear ). mConfig does not protect secrets in process memory . Whoever can read the memory of the process - a heap dump, a debugger, an agent attached to the JVM, other code running in the same process, the operating-system user the process runs as - can read the secrets the application has loaded. Erasing (see Memory wiping ) shortens the time a value is held, which limits what a later heap dump contains; it is no protection against an attacker with access to the running process. Protecting secrets from the process itself takes handles instead of values, such as keys kept in an HSM or a KMS.
docs.title: What mConfig protects against, and what not

docs.text: Ideally, an application never handles raw secrets, but operates via handles only. This is the model of the JCE (Java Cryptography Extension) and of Hardware Security Modules (HSMs): keys stay in a hardware enclave and are used in a controlled manner, without ever entering application memory. Many common tasks, however - sending a bearer token to an API, a password to a database driver - require the actual secret value. mConfig acts as bridge for both: High Security: Manage IDs and handles for HSM/KMS providers. Practical Utility: fetch and provide plaintext tokens or passwords for legacy interfaces, with the exposure limited as described below.
docs.title: Bridging Modern and Legacy security

docs.text: mConfig secrets are treated differently than standard configuration to reduce their exposure footprint: Masking : secret values are replaced by [REDACTED] in logs, toString() and tool output. Transport : the network sources use TLS. The Vault and Kubernetes modules send the Kubernetes ServiceAccount token only to an https address, unless insecure transport is explicitly allowed for development. Other credentials, such as a static Vault token, go to the address you configure: configure an https address. Memory : secret values are handed out as SecretValue , a mutable byte buffer that the application can wipe with erase() , instead of an immutable String . Late-bound decryption : in the configuration, a secret is a reference. It is resolved - fetched, and decrypted where its source keeps it encrypted - only when the application requests the value ( getSecret() ), and the visible bytes can be erased right after use. Status: this is the model the secrets handling is built for. The storages shipped today still fetch their secrets when the configuration is built; fetching on request (lazy fetch) is scheduled for 0.9.1. Strings are immutable and stay on the heap until garbage collected, so a password kept as a String cannot be wiped. A SecretValue can. This works only as far as the value was never a String along the way: values read from text formats ( .properties , JSON, YAML, …) pass through the format parser as String s, and environment variables are String s in the JVM from the start. The buffer reduces the exposure; it does not remove it.
docs.title: mConfig Secrets Handling

docs.text: Vault and AWS Secrets Manager are polled for changes ( pollInterval ; default 60 s for Vault, 5 min for AWS, where API calls have costs; 0 disables polling). The Kubernetes module watches the ConfigMaps and Secrets it reads. Changed values replace the old ones without a process restart, so rotated credentials are picked up.
docs.title: Dynamic Updates

docs.text: When a Configuration is closed via close() , mConfig calls erase() on its configuration layers. The in-memory and default layers and the environment-variable, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and Kubernetes storages wipe the secret buffers they hold. Layers read from files do not wipe yet ; complete wipe-on-close is planned for 0.9.1. With the storages shipped with mConfig, each getSecret() returns a new copy, so wiping it with erase() after use affects only the application's copy, never the stored value. A third-party secrets provider (see Where secrets come from ) should do the same.
docs.title: Memory wiping

docs.text: mConfig distinguishes two kinds of confidentiality. They are related, but they are protected for different reasons and therefore handled differently. SECRET — cryptographic secrets and credentials: private keys, symmetric keys, API tokens, passwords, license IDs. If one leaks, a system is compromised. SENSITIVE — information that must not become visible where it does not belong, typically personal data under GDPR and comparable regimes: names, e-mail addresses, postal addresses, user IDs, IP addresses. If one leaks, a person is harmed and a reporting obligation may follow. The two overlap: most SECRET entries are also SENSITIVE, but far from every SENSITIVE entry is SECRET. A per-user API token is both a credential and personal data. A customer's e-mail address is personal data and no credential at all. The two markers are therefore independent, not a severity scale — an entry may carry either, both, or neither, and when both are set the protections add up.
docs.title: Secret and Sensitive

docs.text: SECRET minimises exposure in time . SENSITIVE minimises exposure in scope . A credential is dangerous for as long as it exists in readable form, so mConfig wraps it, keeps it out of the JVM String pool, and wipes it once it is no longer needed. Personal data is not made safe by wiping it — the application legitimately needs it for its normal working life — but it must not spread into logs, exports, diagnostic dumps, or documentation. This is why SENSITIVE deliberately does not use the SecretValue machinery. Forcing personal data through a wipeable byte buffer would be counterproductive: the application would convert it straight back into a String to use it, and nothing would be gained.
docs.title: The distinction in one sentence

docs.text: What gets suppressed is the value . Where the value is stored always remains traceable. mConfig can tell you, for any entry, which scope and which concrete location it came from — getScope() , getLocation() and getURI() on a ConfigEntry answer this regardless of whether the entry is SECRET, SENSITIVE, or neither. That property is deliberate and is kept intact by every confidentiality mechanism in the library. This matters most precisely for the data that is most protected: Data subjects can exercise their rights. Finding, correcting, and erasing personal data (GDPR Art. 15-17) is only possible if one can determine where the data is held. A redaction that also hid the storage location would obstruct the very obligations SENSITIVE exists to serve. Owners keep authority over their data. If a value comes from "somewhere" and its origin cannot be determined, part of the ownership over it is lost. Credentials can be rotated and revoked. Knowing which store holds a secret is a precondition for replacing or removing it. So a redacted log line or diagnostic dump still names the key, the scope, and the storage location of a protected entry — it withholds only the value itself. Location traceability across a ten-tier hierarchy of heterogeneous sources is a distinguishing property of mConfig, and confidentiality markers do not trade it away.
docs.title: Confidentiality never hides the location

docs.text: 3.1 Writing Configurations ¶ Most of the time, we just read configs from software. After all, they are how software gets told where to find things and how to behave. But if you want to make things more comfortable, you'd also want to write configs. One main difference from reading is that it is less automatic; it can't be. When writing a config, you must specify the Scope. Otherwise, we'd have the writes all over the place, users overwriting each other's settings, and so on. So, you specify which Scope you are about to write. 3.1.1 Writing Priorities ¶ mConfig follows the "principle of least surprise" when writing to a scope: 1. Priority 1 : If an entry for the key already exists in a writeable layer within the scope, that entry is updated. 2. Priority 2 : If the key is new, it is added to the highest-priority writeable layer already available in the scope. 3. Priority 3 : Only if no writeable layers exist is a new configuration file/storage created. What's half-automatic is the format and location. We can use the hierarchy used for reading in writing as well, and we have a default format preference list. But for your specific project, conventions may be different. 3.1.2 Format caveats when writing ¶ Some formats allow extraneous information to be added manually, which is invisible from code. e.g. Java Properties allow comments, but its .load() function omits all of them. So if you do a load() followed by a store(), the comments will be gone in the stored version. You may want to think about this aspect when designing your application. mConfig helps you in this regard with layers and Scopes. 3.1.3 Type Preservation (Planned) ¶ Current : String-first impl ( String.valueOf(value) ) for simplicity. Planned : Pass typed objects to formats (e.g., unquoted numbers/booleans in JSON/YAML). See devdocs/type_preservation_plan.md . 3.1.4 Write Cache (Planned) ¶ For batch writes, enable cache via future ENABLE_CONFIG_CACHE feature, then flush() to persist. flush() will write cache and invalidate read cache.
docs.title: 3.1 Writing Configurations
