docs.text: 3.2 Updates ¶ mConfig automatically detects and uses updates in the configuration sources. Thus, if you access Configuration contents, you'll receive the current values. Conversely, if you store the values you got from the mConfig Configuration in a local variable, that variable won't receive updates, of course. Now for the details. 3.2.1 Update notifications ¶ While the easiest way to use mConfig is just to get() from the Configuration whenever you need a value - there are library objects created using the values values, where you can't pass an mConfig handle. You would need to reinstantiate these, or do similar things. For this purpose, you can subscribe to changes, providing a callback which will get executed when a change occurs. 3.2.1.1 Location-level updates ¶ Configuration.subscribeToUpdates(Consumer<ConfigLocation> listener) Configuration.unsubscribeFromUpdates(Consumer<ConfigLocation> listener) The callback will be executed when any of the Configuration layers in the specified scopes gets changed content. Note on initial discovery: For subscribers, the transition from a non-existent entry to its first assigned value is treated as a change event. This ensures that dynamic entry creation is captured correctly. By default, the scopes exclude RUNTIME, because that's what you set yourself at runtime. The callback is provided as parameter with the ConfigLocation where the change occurred. (You can get the scope from it, e.g.) 3.2.1.2 Entry-level updates ¶ Configuration.subscribeToUpdates(String fullKey, Consumer<ConfigLocation> listener) Subscribe to changes of individual entries by their full key. The callback is called with the ConfigLocation where the entry change was detected. Unsubscribe with Configuration.unsubscribeFromUpdates(Consumer<ConfigLocation> listener) when you don't need it anymore; this feature requires a bit of CPU time when active. 3.2.2 Update settings ¶ To reduce overhead, mConfig limits periodic checks for new content to every x milliseconds. You can configure this with the feature ConfigFeature.UPDATE_CHECK_FREQUENCY_MS (defaults to 2000 ms). Setting UPDATE_CHECK_FREQUENCY_MS to 0 disables the background check thread. Checks then run synchronously on every value access instead, which costs more per read; use it only when you need changes to be visible immediately. 3.2.3 Known issues (0.8.17) ¶ Change detection has known defects, to be fixed in 0.8.18 (MLIB-129). They are not new; all earlier releases have them. Several instances watching one source. A source reports a change once, to the first Configuration that checks it. Where more than one Configuration instance watches the same source, for example the same configuration opened with different schemas in one factory, the others may not reload it and their subscribers may not be notified. Avoid this by keeping one instance per configuration where you rely on updates. Kubernetes (Fabric8 storage): watch lost after an error. If the Kubernetes API closes a watch with an error and the client gives up reconnecting, changes to that ConfigMap or Secret are not detected until a configuration that uses it is opened again. No event is recorded. Files created after subscribing. Subscribers are attached to the layers present when they subscribe; a configuration file created later does not notify them.

Checks then run synchronously on every value access instead, which costs more per read; use it only when you need changes to be visible immediately.
docs.title: 3.2.2 Update settings

docs.text: Change detection has known defects, to be fixed in 0.8.18 (MLIB-129). They are not new; all earlier releases have them. Several instances watching one source. A source reports a change once, to the first Configuration that checks it. Where more than one Configuration instance watches the same source, for example the same configuration opened with different schemas in one factory, the others may not reload it and their subscribers may not be notified. Avoid this by keeping one instance per configuration where you rely on updates. Kubernetes (Fabric8 storage): watch lost after an error. If the Kubernetes API closes a watch with an error and the client gives up reconnecting, changes to that ConfigMap or Secret are not detected until a configuration that uses it is opened again. No event is recorded. Files created after subscribing. Subscribers are attached to the layers present when they subscribe; a configuration file created later does not notify them.

docs.text: 3.3 Getting Information ¶ 3.3.1 Locations: Potential vs. Instantiated ¶ mConfig makes a clear architectural distinction between candidate / potential search locations and active / instantiated layers : 3.3.1.1 Potential Search List ( getSearchList() ) ¶ Where is the overall ConfigFactory looking across all scopes and storage providers? ConfigFactory.getSearchList() returns the ordered list of all candidate ConfigLocation instances. Candidate directories remain in this search list even if they do not exist on disk at initialization time. If a user or process creates one of these directories or files later while the application runs, background change checkers detect it and automatically bind the new configuration. List<ConfigLocation> searchList = configFactory.getSearchList(); System.out.println("Search list (candidate locations):"); for (ConfigLocation location : searchList) { System.out.println("\t" + location.getScope() + "\t" + location.getStorageName() + "\t" + location.getURI("configName", null)); } 3.3.1.2 Active Source Locations ( getSourceLocations() ) ¶ To see which locations actually exist and contributed active data layers to a specific loaded Configuration : Configuration cfg = configFactory.getConfig("network"); System.out.println("Active source locations:"); for (ConfigLocation location : cfg.getSourceLocations()) { System.out.println("\t" + location.getScope() + "\t" + location.getURI("network", null)); } 3.3.1.3 Discovered Configurations ( listAvailableConfigurations() ) ¶ To scan candidate locations and list all configuration files that currently exist with their metadata: Set<ConfigDiscoveryInfo> discovered = configFactory.listAvailableConfigurations(); for (ConfigDiscoveryInfo info : discovered) { System.out.println(info.getConfigName() + " (" + info.getFormat() + ") in " + info.getScope()); } 3.3.2 Legacy support: BLOBs, and where to put files? ¶ Use Configuration mechanisms where possible; this enables all the features, including schema checking, network storage, and so on. 3.3.2.1 Raw Files (Text and Binary) ¶ You may need to access the entire content of a file as a single String or byte array. mConfig provides two specialized formats for this purpose: text_file and binary_file . Reading a text file as a single String: By using the text_file format, the entire file content is read into a single entry with an empty key "" . try (ConfigFactory factory = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("myCompany", "myApplication") .setFeature(ConfigFeature.FILE_FORMAT_READING_PRIORITIES, List.of("text_file")) .build()) { Configuration cfg = factory.getConfig("myTextFile"); String content = cfg.getString(""); } Reading a binary file as a byte array: The binary_file format works similarly but provides the content as a byte array. try (ConfigFactory factory = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("myCompany", "myApplication") .setFeature(ConfigFeature.FILE_FORMAT_READING_PRIORITIES, List.of("binary_file")) .build()) { Configuration cfg = factory.getConfig("myBinaryFile"); byte[] content = cfg.getBytes(""); } 3.3.2.2 Hierarchical BLOBs ¶ In modern formats like JSON and YAML, binary data can be part of the hierarchical structure. JSON (Base64): If a ConfigSchema defines a key as type BYTES , mConfig will automatically decode a Base64-encoded string in a JSON file. YAML (!!binary): YAML supports binary data natively using the !!binary tag. mConfig will correctly retrieve these as byte arrays. byte[] data = cfg.getBytes("server/certificate"); 3.3.2.3 Legacy BLOBs ¶ The second fallback for supporting legacy applications is that you can get filesystem paths for a given Scope. If there are several for the same Scope, mConfigUtil will prioritize the most specific entry, and prefer those which exist already over those which would need to be created. Path localPath = ConfigUtil.whereToPutMyFiles(configFactory, ConfigScope.USER, false); But please, consider using regular mConfig functionality instead where possible.

docs.text: 3.4 Definitions and valid values ¶ 3.4.1 Configuration names ¶ Configuration names identify which configuration to access. This needs to be portable across different storage backends and platforms (files, environment variables, JAR resources, etc.). These rules aim to minimize surprises and increase security. null is not allowed and will result in an error. The empty string "" is technically allowed, but reserved for internal aggregation use cases. Avoid using "" in normal application code. Whitespace handling Leading and trailing whitespace are actively omitted. Multiple internal whitespace characters collapse to a single space. on some backends, whitespace is replaced by underscores. Allowed characters (portable set) Letters A–Z, a–z Digits 0–9 Dot . Underscore _ Hyphen - Space In regex form: [A-Za-z0-9._- ] (spaces are allowed) Some sources (e.g. Filesystem) may sanitize dot usage to guard against path traversal attacks. Configuration names are case sensitive. Examples Valid: "testconfig", "my.config", "my_config", "my-config", "My Config", "prod.v2" invalid: "my/config", "my:config", "my*config", "conf|g", "config<>", "config\tname" 3.4.2 File and directory names from the filesystem ¶ Names that come from the filesystem or the operating system, rather than from the application, are checked as well. Since 0.8.15 the filesystem storage does not use: a search directory whose path contains control characters (line breaks, tabs, escape sequences, other C0/C1 controls), Unicode line or paragraph separators, or bidirectional-override characters. This covers directories from environment variables ( HOME , XDG_CONFIG_HOME , APPDATA , …), from settings such as ADDITIONAL_USER_DIRECTORIES , and test-mode directories. The directory is not added to the search list; a WARNING names it. a .d fragment (a file in <config>.d/ ) whose file name contains such characters. It is skipped with a WARNING and a config event ( SKIPPED_UNREADABLE , detail code FS_DISCOVERY_UNSAFE_NAME ). Such names are never legitimate for configuration, and they could forge or garble log output. Rename the file or directory to use it. See also Outside text in log messages .

docs.text: 3.5 Handling Secrets ¶ mConfig provides a secure way to handle sensitive information like passwords and keys. Background ¶ For the security philosophy and rationale behind secrets handling, see Secrets Concept . 3.5.1 Retrieving Secrets ¶ The getSecret(key) method returns a SecretValue object, which provides safe access to the sensitive data. SecretValue dbPassword = cfg.getSecret("database/password"); if (dbPassword != null) { char[] passwordChars = dbPassword.getChars(); // Use passwordChars ... // Note: SecretValue.erase() can be used to clear internal buffers dbPassword.erase(); } 3.5.2 Schema Integration ¶ To ensure an entry is treated as a secret, set "SECRET": true on its entry in your ConfigSchema . [ { "KEY": "database/password", "TYPE": "STRING", "DESCRIPTION": "Database connection password", "SECRET": true } ] A schema file is a JSON array of entry objects , each carrying its own KEY . An object keyed by configuration key — {"database/password": {...}} — parses to an empty schema without raising an error, so the entry would silently not be protected. Warning: "FLAGS": ["SECRET"] does not mark an entry as secret. The flag is stored but never consulted; all secret handling reads the separate SECRET property. Use "SECRET": true . Since 0.8.15, loading a schema that uses the flag without "SECRET": true logs a WARNING naming the entry. See Which markers are enforced today . Note the difference between a secret and merely sensitive data: SECRET is for cryptographic secrets and passwords, while SENSITIVE marks information that must not leak into view, such as personal data under GDPR. Most secrets are also sensitive, but not the other way round. See Secret and Sensitive . SENSITIVE is defined but not yet enforced, so do not rely on it for compliance today. When an entry is marked as a secret: - It is automatically redacted in logs and toString() calls. - getSecret() returns it as a SecretValue , a byte buffer you can wipe with erase() , instead of a String . - Wiping : when the configuration is closed, the in-memory, environment-variable, Vault, AWS and Kubernetes layers zero the buffers holding the secret. Layers read from files do not yet (planned for 0.9.1). See Memory wiping . mConfig prevents accidental disclosure; it does not protect secrets from anyone who can read the memory of the process. See What mConfig protects against, and what not . 3.5.3 Storage Considerations ¶ mConfig limits how secrets are exposed inside the application; it does not make the underlying storage secure. Secure Stores : Prefer HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Kubernetes Secrets for production credentials. These provide encryption-at-rest and access auditing. Non-Secure Stores : If you store a secret in the Windows Registry , Environment Variables , or Plain Text Files , mConfig will still treat it as a secret inside the application (redacting it, allowing erasure), but the data remains as secure as the storage itself (e.g., Registry ACLs or OS user permissions). Secrets stored in plain-text files are a legitimate setup: their protection is who may read the file. When mConfig writes to such a file ( put() , mconfig set ), the secrets in it stay intact. 3.5.4 Secrets in Exports and Tool Output ¶ Secret values never leave their storage except into the application itself. The rules and their rationale are in Where secret values may appear ; in practice: ConfigMapper.saveTo() writes every entry except secrets. The omitted keys are reported as a WARNING event with detail code EXPORT_SECRETS_OMITTED : java mapper.saveTo(config, Paths.get("export.json")); config.getEvents().stream() .filter(e -> "EXPORT_SECRETS_OMITTED".equals(e.getDetailCode())) .forEach(e -> System.err.println(e.getMessage())); // names the keys, never the values The mconfig CLI shows [REDACTED] instead of a secret value in every command and output format; key, scope and source stay visible. mconfig get also reports Secret: yes ( "secret": true in JSON, YAML and TOML). Reveal a single value on explicit request: bash mconfig mycompany:myapp:database get password --reveal ConfigUtil.copyPrefixedEntriesToJavaProperties() and copySchemeDefinedEntriesToJavaProperties() copy secrets in plain text by design, for in-process hand-over to legacy interfaces such as database drivers. Do not log, store or export the resulting Properties . 3.5.5 Binary Secrets and Crypto Libraries ¶ mConfig seamlessly integrates with JCE and other crypto libraries. You can store raw key bytes as BYTES entries and retrieve them as SecretValue . // Retrieving a private key SecretValue privKeySecret = cfg.getSecret("server/privateKey"); byte[] keyBytes = privKeySecret.getValue(); // Reconstruct the key using JCE KeyFactory kf = KeyFactory.getInstance("RSA"); PrivateKey privKey = kf.generatePrivate(new PKCS8EncodedKeySpec(keyBytes)); 3.5.6 Where secrets come from ¶ A secret is either marked in the schema ( "SECRET": true ) for an entry from any storage, or delivered by a source that knows it is secret. For the second case there are two routes. 1. Secret-aware storage modules. This is the route in use today. Vault ( mconfigsourcevault ), AWS Secrets Manager ( mconfigsourceawssecretsmanager ) and Kubernetes ( mconfigsourcekubernetes , mconfigsourcekubernetesfabric8 ) are storages like the filesystem one: add the module, configure it in its bootstrap configuration ( vault.properties , aws.properties , …; see each module's README), and its entries take part in the scope hierarchy. Entries from Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and Kubernetes Secrets arrive marked secret; Kubernetes ConfigMaps do not. They are opt-in : neither mconfigbasic nor mconfigstandard contains them. Add the dependency explicitly. Vault and AWS Secrets Manager sources default to the CLOUD scope. Their source builders take another scope ( VaultConfigSource.builder().withScope(...) , then addSource(...) ). POLICY : a source the application registers at POLICY scope fails in productive mode unless ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS is set in code. See POLICY locations registered by the application . 2. Secrets providers. Core defines the extension point ConfigSecretsProviderInterface ; providers are found with ServiceLoader and activated with ConfigFactoryBuilder.addSecretsProvider(id, config, scope) . mconfigsecrets (part of mconfigbasic ) places each active provider in the scope hierarchy at the requested scope. It is meant for backends that hand out individual secrets on request, such as a KMS or an HSM. mConfig ships no provider ; the interface is for your own or third-party implementations. A provider should return a new SecretValue per request, so that erase() by the caller does not wipe its stored value.

docs.text: 3.6 Windows Registry Access ¶ mConfig provides two alternative modules for accessing the Windows Registry. Both support reading configuration data from HKEY_CURRENT_USER (USER scope), HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (MACHINE scope), and Group Policy Objects (GPO) in both hives (POLICY scope). 3.6.1 Choosing the Right Module ¶ Feature mConfigWinRegistry mConfigWinRegistryJNI Technology JNR-FFI (Dynamic Native) JNI (Java Native Interface) Artifact Size ~13 KB ~47 KB (includes DLL) Runtime Size ~1.5 MB (includes dependencies) ~47 KB Dependencies JNR-FFI, ASM, JFFI None Complexity Zero (no DLL to manage) Medium (DLL handling) Build Req. Standard Java/Maven Linux + MinGW-w64 (for DLL) Performance High Very High mConfigWinRegistry (JNR-FFI based) ¶ This module is the easiest to use as it requires no native toolchain and handles native access dynamically. - Pros : No native binaries to manage; works out-of-the-box. - Cons : Significantly larger footprint (~1.5 MB) due to the JNR-FFI ecosystem. - Requirement : Java 11+. mConfigWinRegistryJNI (JNI based) ¶ This module provides the smallest footprint and highest performance by using a custom-built DLL. - Pros : Extremely lightweight; no external dependencies. - Cons : Requires building a DLL on Linux (cross-compiled for Windows); the DLL must be provided to the end-user (usually bundled in the JAR). - Requirement : Windows DLL ( mConfigWinRegistryJNI.dll ). - Signing : The bundled DLL is provided unsigned . For production deployments, application developers are responsible for signing the DLL as part of their distribution to establish a "Chain of Trust". 3.6.2 Priority and Discovery ¶ If both modules are present on the classpath, mConfig defaults to using mConfigWinRegistryJNI ( registryjni ) over mConfigWinRegistry ( registry ) for better performance. To use a specific one, you can configure STORAGE_TYPE_PRIORITIES : try (ConfigFactory factory = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("company", "app") .setFeature(ConfigFeature.STORAGE_TYPE_PRIORITIES, List.of("registryjni")) // Force JNI .build()) { // ... } 3.6.3 Base Path Configuration ¶ By default, the registry source looks under Software\\[<CompanyName>\\\\]<ApplicationName> (company segment omitted if COMPANY_NAME blank/null/whitespace). You can override this using the REGISTRY_BASE_PATH feature. You can use the module-specific feature classes, or a string-based key to avoid a compile-time dependency on a specific implementation: // Option 1: Using module-specific classes // For mConfigWinRegistry builder.setFeature(WinRegistryFeatures.REGISTRY_BASE_PATH, "Software\\LegacyPath\\App"); // For mConfigWinRegistryJNI builder.setFeature(WinRegistryJNIFeatures.REGISTRY_BASE_PATH, "Software\\LegacyPath\\App"); // Option 2: Using a string key (works for both modules) builder.setFeature("REGISTRY_BASE_PATH", "Software\\LegacyPath\\App");

You can use the module-specific feature classes, or a string-based key to avoid a compile-time dependency on a specific implementation: // Option 1: Using module-specific classes // For mConfigWinRegistry builder.setFeature(WinRegistryFeatures.REGISTRY_BASE_PATH, "Software\\LegacyPath\\App"); // For mConfigWinRegistryJNI builder.setFeature(WinRegistryJNIFeatures.REGISTRY_BASE_PATH, "Software\\LegacyPath\\App"); // Option 2: Using a string key (works for both modules) builder.setFeature("REGISTRY_BASE_PATH", "Software\\LegacyPath\\App");

docs.text: 3.7 Extensions and Advanced Use ¶ 3.7.1 Extensions and Advanced Features ¶ mConfig allows you to extend its functionality by adding new configuration features without modifying the core library. This is useful for building custom storage backends or format providers. 3.7.1.1 ConfigFeatureBase ¶ To create a new feature, use ConfigFeatureBase . It provides a standard implementation of ConfigFeatureInterface that defines the feature name, value type, and optional default value. import org.metabit.platform.support.config.ConfigFeature; import org.metabit.platform.support.config.ConfigFeatureBase; import org.metabit.platform.support.config.ConfigFeatureInterface; import org.metabit.platform.support.config.ConfigFeatureRegistry; public class MyModuleFeatures { public static final ConfigFeatureInterface MY_SETTING = new ConfigFeatureBase("MY_MODULE_SETTING", ConfigFeature.ValueType.STRING, "default_val"); static { // Register the feature so it can be set by its string name ConfigFeatureRegistry.register(MY_SETTING); } } By registering the feature in the ConfigFeatureRegistry , you enable the library to: 1. Validate values set via string names: builder.setFeature("MY_MODULE_SETTING", "custom_val") . 2. Access the feature without a direct dependency on the module's feature class. 3. Support "self-configuration" via the component's .config/<company>/<application>/mconfig.properties (module features are level ANY unless the module overrides getSettingLevel() ). 4. Provide case-insensitive lookups (ignoring underscores and case). For example, a user of your module could configure it without importing MyModuleFeatures : ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "App") .setFeature("MY_MODULE_SETTING", "some-value"); 3.7.1.2 Writing Custom Extensions ¶ For details on implementing custom ConfigStorageInterface or ConfigFormatInterface , please refer to the developer documentation in project devdocs/library_development.md (not included in public docs). For common utility adapters (Properties, Overrides, Remapping), see 3.9 Utilities and Adapters . 3.7.2 Advanced use ¶ Why perform parameter validation, checks for presence of mandatory settings, generation of parameter documentation yourself? mConfig has a built-in facility for this and more. You describe all the entries your configuration can have, and mConfig takes care of the checking. 3.7.3 Data types ¶ 3.7.3.1 Config schema formats ¶ 3.7.3.1.1 Internal format 0: single ConfigSchemaEntry ¶ { "key":"mandatory key / configuration entry name", "TYPE":"mandatory type", "DEFAULT":"optional default value, as string", "DESCRIPTION":"optional description, for the documentation", "DESCRIPTION":{"en":"English description", "de":"Deutsche Beschreibung"}, "PATTERN":"optional validation pattern", "SCOPES":[ "optional", "scopes", "this", "is", "valid", "in"], "FLAGS":["flags"], "SECRET":false, "HIDDEN":false } Multi-language descriptions are supported by providing a map of language codes to description texts. When requested via getDescription(Locale) , the library will first check this map, then fall back to standard ResourceBundle lookup (using .config/messages.properties ), and finally fall back to the single string description if provided. PLAN : For FLAGS, in the future we may choose an alternative form – each being a pair with string key and boolean value. 3.7.3.1.2 Internal format 1: ConfigSchemas, in an array. internal use only! ¶ [ SCHEME_ENTRIES, GO_HERE, DEFINED_AS_IN_FORMAT_1 ] 3.7.3.1.3 Format 2: full single ConfigSchema ¶ { "name":"mandatory name the Configuration is identified by", "entries":[ ENTRIES_AS_DEFINED_IN_FORMAT_2 ], } 3.7.3.1.4 Format 3: multiple full ConfigSchemas ¶ [ FULL_CONFIG_SCHEMA_AS_DEFINED_IN_FORMAT_3 ] stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> UNDECIDED UNDECIDED --> ARRAY : on [ UNDECIDED --> SCHEME: on { SCHEME --> SCHEME_ENDED : on } SCHEME --> ENTRY_KEY: on string ENTRY --> SCHEME: on next value 3.7.4 configure priorities ¶ 3.7.4.1 File Type Priority ¶ You can control the resolution priority between different file types (e.g. JSON, YAML) using the FILE_TYPE_PRIORITIES feature. This re-orders the search list within each scope. 3.7.4.2 Storage Type Priority ¶ You can control the resolution priority between different storage types (e.g. Files vs. Registry) using the STORAGE_TYPE_PRIORITIES feature. This re-orders the search list within each scope. ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("company", "app") .setFeature(ConfigFeature.STORAGE_TYPE_PRIORITIES, List.of("files", "registry", "registryjni", "JAR")); try (ConfigFactory factory = builder.build()) { // ... } Default IDs include: RAM , secrets , files , registry , registryjni , JAR . Additional directories provided via features like ADDITIONAL_USER_DIRECTORIES are typically prepended to the search list for their scope. This makes them the preferred location for creating new configuration files, while still allowing default files in standard locations to provide values (unless the same key is defined in the additional directory).

docs.text: 3.10 Better Practice: Replace This With That ¶ A list of things to replace by better practice, for people and for AI coding assistants. Each item shows the code to look for, what to write instead, and why. Part 1 is for code that does not use mConfig yet: boilerplate you can delete. Part 2 is for code that uses mConfig, but in a way that works against it. The code to copy is in examples/snippets.md ("templates" below); names and settings are in the Snippets Reference . Part 1: Replace your own boilerplate with mConfig ¶ 1.1 Loading a properties file by hand ¶ Instead of: Properties defaults = new Properties(); try (InputStream in = getClass().getClassLoader().getResourceAsStream("defaultconfig.properties")) { defaults.load(in); } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } Do this: put the file into src/main/resources/.config/<company>/<app>/network.properties and read through mConfig. Configuration net = factory.getConfig("network"); Why: mConfig finds defaults in the JAR by itself and layers the files of the host, the user and the environment on top. The loading block goes away entirely. Template: "Bootstrap". 1.2 A hand-written list of places to look ¶ Instead of: File file = new File(System.getProperty("user.home"), ".myapp/config.properties"); if (!file.exists()) { file = new File("/etc/myapp/config.properties"); } Do this: nothing. The search list is built in. Configuration cfg = factory.getConfig("config"); Why: mConfig knows the standard locations of each operating system ( ~/.config , /etc , %APPDATA% , %PROGRAMDATA% , the registry, …) and their order of precedence. mconfig <company>:<app> search-paths lists them. 1.3 Detecting the operating system to find the configuration directory ¶ Instead of: String os = System.getProperty("os.name").toLowerCase(); Path dir = os.contains("win") ? Paths.get(System.getenv("APPDATA"), "MyApp") : Paths.get(System.getProperty("user.home"), ".config", "myapp"); Do this: for reading, nothing (see 1.2). For a directory to write your own files to: Path dir = ConfigUtil.whereToPutMyFiles(factory, ConfigScope.USER, true); Why: the rules differ per platform and change over time; mConfig keeps them in one place. 1.4 Reading environment variables or system properties directly ¶ Instead of: String host = System.getenv("MYAPP_HOST"); int port = Integer.parseInt(System.getProperty("myapp.port", "8080")); Do this: add mconfigsourceenvvar (part of mconfigstandard ) and read the configuration. String host = net.getString("server/host"); Integer port = net.getInteger("server/port"); Why: the variable MYAPP_NETWORK_SERVER_HOST then overrides the files without any code, the default lives in the schema, and the tool can show where a value came from. Template: "Environment variables". 1.5 Defaults and validation as if chains ¶ Instead of: String value = props.getProperty("port"); int port = (value == null) ? 8080 : Integer.parseInt(value); if (port < 1 || port > 65535) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("port out of range"); } Do this: declare it once in network.mconfig-schema.json , then read it. [ { "KEY": "server/port", "TYPE": "NUMBER", "DEFAULT": 8080, "PATTERN": "uint16" } ] Integer port = net.getInteger("server/port"); Why: name, type, limits, default and description sit in one place, apply wherever the value is read, and can be turned into documentation. Template: "Defaults: schema and resource file". 1.6 A file watcher or a restart to pick up changes ¶ Instead of: WatchService watcher = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService(); configDir.register(watcher, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY); // ... a thread that waits, reloads the file and swaps the values ... Do this: read the value when you need it; subscribe only if you must react. net.subscribeToUpdates(location -> connectionPool.resize(net.getInteger("pool/size"))); Why: mConfig checks its sources for changes (every UPDATE_CHECK_FREQUENCY_MS ) and the next read returns the new value. Template: "Hot reload". 1.7 Passwords as String ¶ Instead of: String password = props.getProperty("db.password"); log.debug("connecting with {}", props); Do this: mark the entry with "SECRET": true in the schema, then: SecretValue password = cfg.getSecret("db/password"); Why: a SecretValue shows as [REDACTED] in logs and toString() , stays out of exports, and can be wiped with erase() . Template: "Secrets". 1.8 Redirecting configuration paths for tests by hand ¶ Instead of: System.setProperty("user.home", tempDir.toString()); // and hope nothing else reads it Do this: ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "demoApp"); builder.setTestMode(true); builder.setTestConfigPaths(ConfigScope.USER, List.of(tempDir.toString())); Why: test mode keeps tests away from the real configuration of the machine and the user, without changing production code. Template: "Tests"; details: Test Mode . Part 2: If you already use mConfig, do it this way ¶ 2.1 A default at the call site ¶ Instead of: Integer port = cfg.getInteger("server/port"); if (port == null) { port = 8080; } Do this: declare "DEFAULT": 8080 in the schema. Integer port = cfg.getInteger("server/port"); Why: a default at the call site is invisible, unvalidated and undocumented, and the second place that reads the key will use a different one. With the default settings a missing value throws ConfigException anyway, so the null check is dead code. 2.2 Parsing or validating by hand ¶ Instead of: int port = Integer.parseInt(cfg.getString("server/port")); Do this: Integer port = cfg.getInteger("server/port"); Why: the typed getters convert, and TYPE and PATTERN in the schema have already checked the value. 2.3 Copying values into fields at startup ¶ Instead of: this.port = cfg.getInteger("server/port"); // in the constructor, used for the lifetime Do this: keep the Configuration and read on use, or subscribe to updates (1.6). int port() { return cfg.getInteger("server/port"); } Why: a copy never changes; hot reload does nothing for it. 2.4 A factory per lookup ¶ Instead of: Configuration c = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "demoApp").build().getConfig("network"); Do this: build one ConfigFactory for the application, share it, close it on shutdown. Why: every factory scans the search locations again and owns watcher threads; a factory that is never closed leaks them. 2.5 A secret read as a string, or marked the wrong way ¶ Instead of: String password = cfg.getString("db/password"); { "KEY": "db/password", "TYPE": "STRING", "FLAGS": ["SECRET"] } Do this: { "KEY": "db/password", "TYPE": "STRING", "SECRET": true } SecretValue password = cfg.getSecret("db/password"); Why: "FLAGS": ["SECRET"] is accepted (with a WARNING) but protects nothing; only "SECRET": true does. And a String cannot be wiped and ends up in a log line sooner or later. 2.6 A dot as separator in hierarchical keys ¶ Instead of: cfg.getString("server.host"); // against a JSON, YAML or TOML file with nested "server" Do this: cfg.getString("server/host"); Why: the separator is / . A dot is part of the key; in flat formats such as .properties the key server.host is one literal name. 2.7 Chaining off setTestMode() ¶ Instead of: ConfigFactory factory = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "demoApp").setTestMode(true).build(); Do this: ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("ACME", "demoApp"); builder.setTestMode(true); ConfigFactory factory = builder.build(); Why: setTestMode() , setTestConfigPaths() and setTestParameters() return void ; the chained form does not compile. Only the setFeature(...) family, setSchemas() , addSource() and addSecretsProvider() return the builder. 2.8 Reading the environment next to mConfig ¶ Instead of: String host = System.getenv("DEMOAPP_NETWORK_SERVER_HOST"); if (host == null) { host = cfg.getString("server/host"); } Do this: String host = cfg.getString("server/host"); Why: with mconfigsourceenvvar the variable already arrives in the SESSION scope and overrides the files. Your own precedence logic duplicates the hierarchy and hides the origin of the value. 2.9 Your own override or fallback logic ¶ Instead of: String value = overrides.containsKey(key) ? overrides.get(key) : cfg.getString(key); Do this: cfg.put(key, value, ConfigScope.RUNTIME); Why: RUNTIME is the scope for in-memory overrides by your own code; it wins over everything except POLICY . Fallback between scopes is built in ( FALLBACKS_ACROSS_SCOPES ). The ConfigUtil.withOverrides() view is for cases where the configuration must not be changed. 2.10 Packing a single JAR with jar-with-dependencies ¶ Instead of: <descriptorRef>jar-with-dependencies</descriptorRef> Do this: use a packaging that merges the META-INF/services files (the merging assembly descriptor, shade's ServicesResourceTransformer , or Shadow's mergeServiceFiles() ). Why: that descriptor keeps one file per service interface, so storages and formats go missing; build() fails with JAVA_SERVICE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR , or sources are lost without notice. Template: "Dependencies"; details: Packaging as a single JAR . 2.11 Library settings in the global mconfig.properties ¶ Instead of: src/main/resources/.config/metabit/mConfig/mconfig.properties Do this: src/main/resources/.config/<company>/<app>/mconfig.properties , or setFeature(...) in code. Why: the global file is deprecated and removed before 0.9.0; a component configures the library for itself only. Features marked CODE_ONLY can be set in code only. 2.12 POLICY locations registered by the application ¶ Instead of: builder.setFeature(ConfigFeature.ADDITIONAL_RUNTIME_DIRECTORIES, List.of("POLICY:/opt/myapp/policy")); Do this: leave POLICY to the administrator's locations (Group Policy, enforced settings). Use HOST or APPLICATION for what the application ships. Why: POLICY overrides everything, so an application must not grant it to itself. Outside test mode such a location fails unless ALLOW_APPLICATION_POLICY_LOCATIONS is set in code. 2.13 A version copied from documentation ¶ Instead of: copying <version>${mconfig.version}</version> , or a version number from an example, into a build file. Do this: take the version the project already uses (its pom.xml , build.gradle , or the local repository). If none can be found, ask. Why: examples age; a placeholder without a definition does not build. Settings that replace manual code ¶ Instead of writing Set checks for keys the schema does not know SCHEMA_STRICT_MODE=true null handling for missing values schema DEFAULT ; EXCEPTION_ON_MISSING_ENTRY decides between exception and null loops over scopes for reading or writing FALLBACKS_ACROSS_SCOPES , WRITE_FALLBACK_ACROSS_SCOPES probing file formats in a fixed order FILE_FORMAT_READING_PRIORITIES , FILE_FORMAT_WRITING_PRIORITIES All settings: Config Features .

docs.text: 3.9 Utilities and Adapters ¶ The mConfigUtil module provides specialized Configuration implementations (adapters) and static utility methods to bridge existing Java structures with the mConfig ecosystem. 3.9.1 Core Adapters ¶ These classes allow existing configuration sources to be viewed through the Configuration interface. 3.9.1.1 PropertiesConfiguration ¶ Used for adapting legacy code step-by-step. It allows programmatically generated java.util.Properties to be integrated into the unified mConfig structure. - Note : This adapter provides almost none of the advanced features mConfig supplies (like multi-tier resolution or automatic schema discovery). - Recommendation : Consider loading properties via mConfig itself by adding paths to ConfigFeature.ADDITIONAL_USER_DIRECTORIES . 3.9.1.2 OverridingConfiguration ¶ Provides an immutable view that overlays a Map<String, Object> on top of an existing Configuration . Overrides take precedence. - Note : This is intended for temporary, in-memory overlays. - Recommendation : For most use cases, prefer using Configuration.put*(key, value, ConfigScope.RUNTIME) . The RUNTIME scope is specifically designed for temporary overrides that are not persisted. 3.9.1.3 RemappedConfiguration ¶ Remaps keys matching a newPrefix to an oldPrefix for lookup in an underlying source configuration. This is useful for maintaining backward compatibility or redirecting configuration branches. 3.9.1.4 What the adapters are, and what they are not ¶ The adapters help with transition and adoption. They are views for reading, not a second facade; for anything beyond that, use the mConfig Configuration itself. Read-only. Every put(...) throws ConfigException with reason NOT_WRITEABLE , with or without a scope; isWriteable() is false . (Up to 0.8.16, RemappedConfiguration wrote through for some put variants.) No cursor , and the schema cannot be set on a view: getConfigCursor() and setConfigSchema() throw UnsupportedOperationException . RemappedConfiguration and OverridingConfiguration show their source as it is. Values, entries, the schema, getSourceLocations() , isClosed() and update subscriptions are those of the configuration behind the view. A secret is handed on as a SecretValue . An entry reports the key, scope and location it has in the source; the schema of a remapped view knows the keys under the old prefix. A remapped view hides what the source has under the new prefix. Every key starting with newPrefix is read from oldPrefix , so a key the source itself has under newPrefix cannot be read through the view; a listing still names it once, since the view shows both under the same name. Choose a newPrefix the source does not use. Overrides are checked when read. An override that cannot be converted to the requested type throws ConfigException ( CONVERSION_FAILURE ); one that does not match the schema of the parent throws ConfigException ( ARGUMENT_INVALID ). The value is not put into the message. An entry from the overrides has no scope and no location ( null ): it was not read from anywhere. PropertiesConfiguration behaves like the Properties behind it. A key that is not there gives null , no exception. A value that cannot be converted to the requested type throws ConfigException ( CONVERSION_FAILURE ), as parsing the string in plain Java would (up to 0.8.16: null ). getSecret() returns the property as a SecretValue (up to 0.8.16: always null ); in the Properties it stays a plain, unprotected String, so the first such access is logged at INFO level, once per JVM, through the JDK's System.Logger named mConfig . Read secrets through mConfig itself. No schema, no locations, no update notifications. 3.9.2 Scope-Restricted Reads ¶ All three adapter classes implement the full Configuration interface, including the scope-aware read methods. Scope restriction is per-call — there is no per-instance scope state — so the same adapter instance can safely serve call sites that need different scope views. The adapters do not treat the scopes alike: Adapter Scope-restricted read RemappedConfiguration passed on to the source: only the given scopes are read OverridingConfiguration an override applies whatever the scopes; keys that are not overridden are read from the parent in the given scopes PropertiesConfiguration the scopes are ignored: Properties have none To read a value only from specific scopes, use getConfigEntryFromFullKey(key, scopes) : EnumSet<ConfigScope> localScopes = EnumSet.of(ConfigScope.PRODUCT, ConfigScope.HOST); Configuration remapped = ConfigUtil.remapped(base, "old.prefix", "new.prefix"); ConfigEntry entry = remapped.getConfigEntryFromFullKey("my.key", localScopes); String value = (entry != null) ? entry.getValueAsString() : null; To enumerate all keys visible in specific scopes: Set<String> keys = config.getAllConfigurationKeysFlattened(localScopes); 3.9.3 ConfigUtil Entry Point ¶ The ConfigUtil class provides convenient factory methods for the adapters above, along with other helper functions: Factory Methods : ConfigUtil.fromProperties(Properties props) ConfigUtil.withOverrides(Configuration parent, Map<String, Object> overrides) ConfigUtil.remapped(Configuration source, String oldPrefix, String newPrefix) Path Discovery : ConfigUtil.whereToPutMyFiles(...) : Helps find writable configuration paths for a given scope. ConfigUtil.printConfigPaths(...) : Prints the discovered configuration search paths for debugging. Property Extraction : ConfigUtil.copyPrefixedEntriesToJavaProperties(...) : Exports a subset of a configuration to a Properties object. ConfigUtil.copySchemeDefinedEntriesToJavaProperties(...) : Exports all entries defined by the configuration schema. Quick Configuration : ConfigUtil.quickConfig(...) : A one-liner for bootstrapping a standard configuration for simple applications. 3.9.4 Usage ¶ Add the following dependency to your project: <dependency> <groupId>org.metabit.platform.support.config</groupId> <artifactId>mConfigUtil</artifactId> <version>${mconfig.version}</version> </dependency> JPMS module name: requires metabit.mconfig.util;

docs.text: 4.1 mConfig Tool ( mconfig ) ¶ The mconfig tool provides a command-line interface for inspecting and managing configurations. It allows you to list available configurations, show effective values, get detailed metadata for specific keys, search for configuration paths, and more. 4.1.1 Installation ¶ The tool is available as a "fat JAR" in the mConfigTools module. You can run it using: java -jar mConfigTools-*.jar [OPTIONS] [COMMAND] [COMMAND_OPTIONS] 4.1.2 Subcommands ¶ list : List all available configurations for the given company and application. show : Print the effective configuration (all keys and values). get : Show detailed information for a specific key (value, type, source URI, scope, and description). search-paths : List all directories and storage locations where mConfig looks for files. set : Set or update a configuration entry. Supports key=value pairs or -K/--key with -V/--value . Requires a target --scope unless implied by schema. monitor : Monitor a configuration for real-time changes. Keeps running until interrupted. Experimental commands ¶ These commands are not complete yet. They are hidden from mconfig --help and refused unless -X / --experimental is given, before or after the command name ( mconfig -X validate … ). Do not rely on their output in automation yet. validate : Validate a configuration against its schema. Checks the effective values only, not the values in each layer. propose-schema : Generate a draft ConfigSchema JSON from an existing configuration. Currently disabled; being rewritten for 0.9.2. kubernetes-rbac : Print a Role and RoleBinding for the ServiceAccount of a pod that reads its configuration through the Kubernetes sources. The output is a broad template: it grants read on all ConfigMaps and Secrets in the namespace. Restrict it with resourceNames to the resources you configured before applying it. A generator limited to the configured resources is planned for 0.9.3. 4.1.2.1 set command options: ¶ -V, --value=<value> : The value to set. Shorthand -V is intentionally used for value (not for version). -K, --key=<key> : The key to set (optional when using key=value positional form). -m, --comment=<text> : Comment to associate with the entry (format support varies; shown with get -v ). -S, --scope=<scope> : Target ConfigScope ( USER , HOST , SESSION , RUNTIME , etc.). -T, --type=<type> : ConfigEntryType (optional, inferred from schema if available). -F, --file-format=<fmt> : Preferred file format when creating a new file (e.g., PROPERTIES , YAML , TOML ). -d, --dry-run : Display what would be changed without performing the actual write. --create : Create missing parent directories and configuration files if they do not exist yet. You can also pass one or more key=value pairs as positional arguments after the vector, e.g. mconfig set acme:app:conf db.port=5432 . N.B.: Some file formats may lose comments on write access. TOML, .INI, and .PROPERTIES are known to be safe. 4.1.2.2 monitor command options: ¶ --dump : Print the full effective configuration before starting the monitor loop. -v, --verbose : Provide more detail about changes (e.g., the scope and source of the change). 4.1.3 Global Options and Commands (verb/vector order) ¶ The tool accepts both orders: - mconfig <verb> <vector> [...options] - mconfig <vector> <verb> [...options] For example, mconfig acme:app:conf show is equivalent to mconfig show acme:app:conf . Options can be placed both before and after the command (verb). -c, --company=<name> : Company name (default: MCONFIG_COMPANY env var). Use "" (empty string) intentionally to omit the company segment in all paths/sources (e.g., ~/.config/myapp/ ). -a, --app=<name> : Application name (default: MCONFIG_APP env var) -C, --config=<name> : Configuration name (default: MCONFIG_CONFIG env var) -K, --key=<name> : Specific configuration key -o, --output=<format> : Output format ( HUMAN , JSON , CSV ) -v, --verbose : Enable verbose output (shows source URIs and scopes) --debug : Enable debug logging for the CLI and underlying library -l, --lang=<lang> : Preferred language for descriptions (default: en ) Do not underestimate the power of "-v" verbose mode! Try it and see which extra information you can get out of it. 4.1.4 Shortened Syntax ¶ For quick interactive use, the tool supports a positional vector in the format: [COMPANY:]APPLICATION[:SUBDIR...]:CONFIGNAME[@KEY] Notes: - COMPANY is optional. Use a leading : to omit it: :myapp:settings . - Optional SUBDIR components map to subdirectories under the application root (per Resource Configuration Layout). - The optional key is introduced with @ to avoid ambiguity: ...:CONFIGNAME@KEY . - Legacy :CONFIGNAME:KEY syntax is no longer supported. Examples: - mconfig mycompany:myapp:database show (with company) - mconfig :myapp:database show (app-only) Both equivalent to mconfig --company [""""] --app myapp --config database show . 4.1.5 Environment Variables ¶ The tool automatically picks up the following environment variables if the corresponding options are not provided: - MCONFIG_COMPANY - MCONFIG_APP - MCONFIG_CONFIG Test/CI note: The CLI does not enable Test Mode by default. For isolated tests, you can direct discovery to temporary directories via the JVM system property TESTMODE_DIRECTORIES (e.g., -DTESTMODE_DIRECTORIES=USER:/tmp/testdir ). 4.1.6 Examples ¶ List configurations: bash mconfig --company mycomp --app myapp list Show effective configuration: bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:settings show # OR mconfig show --company mycomp --app myapp --config settings Get value and metadata for a specific key: bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:db:password get Change output to JSON for scripting: bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:settings show -o JSON See where the values in your configuration are coming from: bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:settings show -v Set a configuration value: bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:db:user set --value="dbuser" --scope=USER Update a configuration value with dry-run and validation: bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:settings:timeout set -V 30 -S HOST -T NUMBER --dry-run Monitor configuration changes: This one's for you, SRE and developers! bash mconfig mycomp:myapp:settings monitor --dump -v mconfig :myapp:settings monitor --dump -v # app-only App-only examples (omit company segment): bash mconfig -c "" myapp list mconfig :myapp:db get password

docs.text: 4.2 Logging in mConfig ¶ mConfig uses a custom logging abstraction defined by the ConfigLoggingInterface . This allows the library to remain independent of specific logging frameworks while still providing necessary diagnostic information. Available Implementations ¶ Implementation Module Priority Service Name Use Case NullLogging mConfigCore 0 null Default; silent operation. ConsoleLogging mConfigCore 1 console Dev/tests; prints to stdout/stderr. Not for production. StdErrLogger mConfigUtil 1 stderr-logger Minimal logger printing to stderr. JavaSystemLogger mConfigUtil 2 java.System.Logger Uses JDK 9+ System.Logger . Slf4j2Logger mConfigLoggingSlf4j 5 slf4j Production use; forwards to SLF4J. Internal and Hidden Implementations ¶ InternalLogger ( mConfigCore , impl.core ): Activated if ConfigFeature.LOGGING_REDIRECT_TARGET is set. Redirects to specified target. Using SLF4J2Logger in Production ¶ Slf4j2Logger (priority 5) bridges mConfig logging to SLF4J. 4.2.1 Add Dependencies ¶ Maven: <dependency> <groupId>org.metabit.platform.support.config</groupId> <artifactId>mConfigLoggingSlf4j</artifactId> <version>${mconfig.version}</version> </dependency> Gradle: implementation 'org.metabit.platform.support.config:mConfigLoggingSlf4j:${mconfig.version}' Note: Also need SLF4J API + impl (e.g., logback-classic). 4.2.2 Auto-Discovery ¶ With mConfigLoggingSlf4j on classpath, auto-selected (highest prio). Override with ConfigFactoryBuilder.setFeature(ConfigFeature.LOGGING_TO_USE_IN_CONFIGLIB, "slf4j") . 4.2.3 Configuration ¶ Configure SLF4J via logback.xml , etc. Slf4j2Logger uses logger name from ConfigFactoryBuilder company/app or default "mConfig". ConsoleLogging for Development and Tests ¶ ConsoleLogging is a lightweight console logger (stdout for lower levels, stderr for WARN/ERROR) for debugging mConfig internals. It is included directly in mConfigCore with no external dependencies required. 4.2.4 Manual Activation ¶ You can instantiate ConsoleLogging directly and pass it to components. import org.metabit.platform.support.config.impl.logging.ConsoleLogging; import org.metabit.platform.support.config.ConfigFeature; // ... in your test ... ConsoleLogging logger = new ConsoleLogging("MyModuleTest"); logger.setLevel("DEBUG"); // Use with a component that takes a logger component.testComponent(settings, logger); 4.2.5 Usage with ConfigFactoryBuilder ¶ ConfigFactoryBuilder uses ServiceLoader to discover ConfigLoggingInterface implementations. ConsoleLogging is discoverable via ServiceLoader and JPMS provides in mConfigCore . To force the use of ConsoleLogging when using ConfigFactoryBuilder in tests or development: ConfigFactoryBuilder builder = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("company", "app"); builder.setFeature(ConfigFeature.LOGGING_TO_USE_IN_CONFIGLIB, "console"); Configuration ¶ Log Levels ¶ Available levels: TRACE , DEBUG , INFO , WARN , ERROR . Default level for ConsoleLogging is INFO . You can set the level via setLevel(String) : logger.setLevel("TRACE"); Output Redirection ¶ INFO , DEBUG , TRACE are printed to System.out . WARN , ERROR are printed to System.err . Outside text in log messages ¶ mConfig logs file names, paths and other names that come from outside the application: from the filesystem, environment variables, or configuration sources. Such text could contain line breaks that forge extra log lines, terminal escape sequences that rewrite a console, or bidirectional overrides that make a name look different from what it is (CWE-117). Since 0.8.15, the filesystem storage writes such text into log messages with these characters escaped: control characters as \n , \r , \t or \uXXXX , Unicode line and paragraph separators and bidi controls as \uXXXX . Everything else, backslashes in Windows paths included, is logged unchanged, so the logged location matches the real one. Names containing such characters are also refused as input; see File and directory names from the filesystem . Limits: Since 0.8.17 the other storages and the format parsers escape outside text the same way, including exception messages they put into a log line. Names are not refused there; escaping only. Exceptions passed to the logger as such, with their stack traces, are not escaped. Lookups that a logging backend performs on message content, e.g. ${...} in old log4j 2 versions, are the backend's responsibility. Use a current backend version. For library and module developers: build messages with org.metabit.platform.support.config.impl.logging.LogSafe.text(value) for every outside value, and never put outside text into the format string of the format variants of ConfigLoggingInterface ; pass it as an argument. Parse errors ¶ When a configuration file or resource cannot be parsed, mConfig logs one WARNING and records a PARSE event. It always names the configuration, the location, the format, the type of error, the line and column, and the key at the error position if the parser can tell it. The file is skipped; other sources still supply their values. A parser's own message often quotes the content it failed on. If that content is a secret value, the message would carry it into the log. Since 0.8.17 the parser's message is therefore added only where the content cannot hold a secret: never for secret stores (e.g. Kubernetes Secrets) and for the bootstrap configurations of the cloud modules ( vault , aws , ...), which typically hold credentials without a schema; not if the configuration's schema marks the entry at the error position, or an entry above or below it, as SECRET ; not if the parser cannot tell the position (e.g. SnakeYAML) and the schema has any SECRET entry. The full list, including the cases that need no schema, is in Secrets: parse errors . The log line then says that the parser details were withheld. For development, set LOG_PARSE_ERROR_DETAILS in code to see every parser message. All of it is escaped like other outside text. How Logging is Discovered and Selected ¶ In DefaultConfigFactoryBuilder.findLoggerForConfigUse() : If ConfigFeature.LOGGING_REDIRECT_TARGET is set, instantiate InternalLogger with target and init. Load ServiceLoader<ConfigLoggingInterface> : Prefer exact match to ConfigFeature.LOGGING_TO_USE_IN_CONFIGLIB by service name (case-insensitive). Otherwise, select highest priority ( getServiceModulePriority() ) among those that init() successfully. Fallback to NullLogging . All loggers must implement init(ConfigFactorySettings) (usually returns true ) and exit() .

docs.text: mConfig logs file names, paths and other names that come from outside the application: from the filesystem, environment variables, or configuration sources. Such text could contain line breaks that forge extra log lines, terminal escape sequences that rewrite a console, or bidirectional overrides that make a name look different from what it is (CWE-117). Since 0.8.15, the filesystem storage writes such text into log messages with these characters escaped: control characters as \n , \r , \t or \uXXXX , Unicode line and paragraph separators and bidi controls as \uXXXX . Everything else, backslashes in Windows paths included, is logged unchanged, so the logged location matches the real one. Names containing such characters are also refused as input; see File and directory names from the filesystem . Limits: Since 0.8.17 the other storages and the format parsers escape outside text the same way, including exception messages they put into a log line. Names are not refused there; escaping only. Exceptions passed to the logger as such, with their stack traces, are not escaped. Lookups that a logging backend performs on message content, e.g. ${...} in old log4j 2 versions, are the backend's responsibility. Use a current backend version. For library and module developers: build messages with org.metabit.platform.support.config.impl.logging.LogSafe.text(value) for every outside value, and never put outside text into the format string of the format variants of ConfigLoggingInterface ; pass it as an argument.

docs.text: 4.3 FAQ - Frequently Asked Questions ¶ 4.3.1 I want to... ¶ I want to extract a subconfiguration to a Properties object. ¶ If your configuration contains a subset of entries, say, for an existing Java component which expects them that way, and you just want to get an pass them on, then ConfigUtil.copyPrefixedEntriesToJavaProperties() is what should help you. You specify the prefix, including possible "." from the hierarchy, and get a java.util.Properties instance with all the contents from the Configuration which start with the prefix. The prefix is removed automatically. Caveat: This will skip configuration layers where the source does not allow enumeration of its contents. So the result of this call may yield results different from what you'd get if you were using the Configuration itself! Recommendation: If that subconfig can be limited in what it may and should contain, please consider using a ConfigSchema (in addition, or instead). Also, have a look at other methods in the ConfigUtil class, for similar use cases. I want to know where my configuration files are located. ¶ Use the mConfigTool provided. It can tell you the general search paths (potential locations), as well as the actual locations of the files it found, and where the values in individual entries come from. Programmatically, mConfig allows you to trace the origin of each individual configuration value you get. If your interest focused on filesystem only, ConfigUtil.whereToPutMyFiles() may be what you are looking for. 4.3.2 Why is... ¶ Why can't I state my defaults right at the place I'm asking for the value? ¶ This approach sounds simpler - getInteger("weightInTons",5) looks good at first sight. Until you realize what happens when you ask for this value a second time, or a third... Also, this prevents you from generating a proper documentation of your configuration parameters. ConfigSchemas should not be hard to use. Try them, please. But if you insist on using the old way, there is the mConfigCheese module - for those who like their code a bit pungent. Coming from Spring: why are there no ${...} placeholders, profiles or conditional values? ¶ Because mConfig answers the same needs by where a value is stored, not by rules inside the configuration. For every entry you can ask which scope and which location it came from ( getScope() , getLocation() , or mconfig get <key> -v ), and the answer is one place. Placeholders, profiles and conditions each break that: the value you read is then computed from several places, or depends on a switch set somewhere else. No ${...} placeholders. A value is what its source says, character by character. A value assembled from other keys has no single origin; "where does this come from?" has no clear answer any more. A reference to another key can pull a secret into a value that is not marked as one, and from there into logs and exports. A $ in a password or a path needs no escaping. If two settings share a part, keep the part as its own entry and combine in code, or store the complete value at the place that differs. No profiles. There is no application-prod.properties and no switch that selects it. What differs between deployments is stored where the deployment is: In Spring In mConfig defaults in application.properties defaults in the JAR ( PRODUCT scope), or DEFAULT in the schema application-prod.properties a file on the production host ( HOST scope, e.g. below /etc ), or values from the cluster or cloud source ( CLUSTER , CLOUD ) a developer's local overrides the user's own file ( USER scope) overrides per container or start environment variables ( SESSION scope) the test profile test mode with src/test/resources/.config/ The JAR is the same everywhere and carries no production values. See Priorities and Hierarchies for the order in which the scopes apply. No conditional values. There is no "if the host is called prod-* " and no @ConditionalOnProperty for values. Which value applies follows from the fixed order of the scopes alone, so the same question gives the same answer, and the tool can show why. mConfig itself runs fine inside a Spring application; see "Spring Boot wiring" in the snippets . 4.3.3 How can I fix... ¶ Quick Verification Checklist ¶ If it's not working yet: Place a test config file: Create ~/.config/myCompany/myApplication/network.properties (Linux/Mac) or %APPDATA%\myCompany\myApplication\network.properties (Windows): peer = localhost port = 8080 probability = 0.5 List discovered configs: java try (ConfigFactory factory = ConfigFactoryBuilder.create("myCompany", "myApplication").build()) { factory.listAvailableConfigurations().forEach(System.out::println); } Enable logging: Add mConfigLoggingSlf4j dep + SLF4J config (see No mConfig logging output below). Use mConfigTool CLI: mconfig myCompany:myApplication get network.peer -v (requires building mConfigTools; see mConfigTools README ). See detailed troubleshooting sections below. Updates to config files are not detected ¶ You are not buffering the results in some local variables, are you? Your own variables are not updated by mConfig. Ask the Configuration object for the value instead whenever you need it. Are the directories and files accessible for the account the program runs as? mConfig needs to be able to list directory contents and read config files; inaccessible dirs and files cause debug messages at most, but no error. The cache setting doesn't match with your expected reaction time. For efficiency, files are not checked and re-read on every config value access. There is a delay between checks. If the default value (2 seconds) is too long for your purposes, you can change it. @TODO name the config settings key. Keep in mind a higher update frequency increases overhead. Is the format supported? You can choose and combine mconfig Format modules; if the file extension pattern of the config file does not match with a file format present in your current build, it won't be read. JPMS Module Access Errors ¶ If your application uses JPMS (named module-info.java ) but omits requires for mConfig modules, you will see access errors. Compile-time (javac): cannot access metabit.mconfig.core.ConfigFactory module your.module does not read module metabit.mconfig.core Runtime (java): java.lang.IllegalAccessError: class your.package.YourClass cannot access class metabit.mconfig.core.ConfigFactory (in module metabit.mconfig.core) because module your.module does not read module metabit.mconfig.core Fix: Add the required requires directives to your module-info.java . The list depends on the mConfig variant: mconfigbasic (JPMS requires section) mconfigstandard (JPMS requires section) mconfigbasicbinary (JPMS requires section) See also JPMS introduction . Config values always returning defaults or null ¶ Symptoms: Calls like cfg.getString("key") return null or schema defaults; no exceptions or warnings. Common causes: - Mismatched company , application , or configName (case-sensitive). - No config files in standard locations (classpath src/main/resources/.config/<company>/<app>/<configName>.properties or filesystem equivalents). - File extension not matching available formats (e.g., .yaml without YAML format module). - Permissions issues on directories/files (check logs). - Application packed into a single JAR without merging META-INF/services files; see Faulty single-JAR packaging below. Fix steps: 1. Use factory.listAvailableConfigurations() to list discovered configs and their sources. 2. Run mConfigTool CLI for full diagnostics: paths searched, files found, entry origins. 3. Verify placements per Getting Started . 4. Add missing format modules (e.g., mConfigFormatYAMLwithJackson for YAML). Faulty single-JAR packaging ¶ Symptoms: the application works when started from the IDE or with mvn exec , but not as a single ("fat") JAR. Either build() fails with JAVA_SERVICE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR: mConfig did not find all of its components, likely due to faulty JAR packaging, ... or values from bundled defaults or from files are missing ( NO_MATCHING_ENTRY ), without any warning. The log line mConfig initialised, ... storages [...] lacks storages you expect, e.g. JAR or files . Cause: the JAR was built by unpacking all dependency JARs into one, without merging their META-INF/services files, e.g. with the jar-with-dependencies descriptor of the Maven assembly plugin. Only one file per service interface survives; which one depends on dependency order. Fix: merge the service files when packaging; see Packaging as a single JAR for the Maven assembly, Maven shade and Gradle configurations. Then test the packaged JAR itself, not only the classes. This is not specific to mConfig: every library that uses ServiceLoader (e.g. SLF4J 2, Log4j 2, JDBC drivers, Jackson modules) is affected. mConfig detects it when its core registrations are among the lost ones and then fails build() with the message above; in other cases nothing reports it, for mConfig or for the other libraries. Tests not loading expected configurations ¶ Symptoms: Unit/integration tests use production defaults or empty configs despite setTestMode(true) . Causes: - Missing ConfigFactoryBuilder.setTestMode(true) before build() . - Test files not in correct locations. - forbidTestMode() called or PERMIT_TEST_MODE=false . Fix: 1. Add @BeforeAll static void setup() { ConfigFactoryBuilder.setTestMode(true); } 2. Place files in: - src/test/resources/.config/<company>/<app>/<configName>.ext (preferred) - src/test/resources/config/<SCOPE> (e.g., USER ) 3. Custom: ConfigFactoryBuilder.setFeature(ConfigFeature.TESTMODE_DIRECTORIES, List.of("USER:src/test/configs")); 4. See full details in Test Mode . No mConfig logging output ¶ Symptoms: Silent on config discovery, errors, or debug info. Fix: 1. Add dependency: mConfigLoggingSlf4j . 2. Configure SLF4J backend (e.g., Logback logback.xml ): xml <logger name="metabit.config" level="DEBUG"/> 3. Ensure SLF4J implementation (logback-classic, log4j-slf4j) on classpath. See Logging . Environment variables don't provide config values ¶ Symptoms: Env vars like myapp-network-peer=localhost ignored. Fix: 1. Add mConfigSourceEnvVar dependency. 2. Use naming schema: <application>_<configName>_<key> , UPPER CASE , e.g. MYAPP_NETWORK_PEER . Within the key, / becomes _ and a literal _ becomes __ . This is the rule of the Elasticsearch ( ES_SETTING_... ) and Confluent Platform (Kafka) Docker images, too. It is close to MicroProfile Config / Quarkus and Grafana: these also separate with _ , but do not double a literal _ , so the names are the same only for keys without an underscore. It is the reverse of the .NET and Airflow custom, though, where __ separates the levels: here MYAPP_NETWORK_DB__HOST is the key db_host , and MYAPP_NETWORK_DB_HOST is db/host . Up to 0.8.16 the underscore was not doubled; a WARNING names a variable still in the old naming. On Linux and macOS env var names are case-sensitive, so a lowercase name is not found. 3. Scope: SESSION (overrides USER). 4. Verify via mConfigTool or enable logging. See mConfigSourceEnvVar README .
